Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Models that suggest sources and magnetic field structures align horizontally may conflict with our observations, while a model featuring inclined sources and magnetic field lines is more consistent with our data. Our research highlights the significance of anisotropy studies in better comprehending the extremely energetic cosmic sphere. To further explore these anisotropies, we propose enhancing the detection capability of next-generation experiments through an anisotropy-focused design approach. Doing so may allow us to uncover more nuanced patterns of anisotropy in the data, which could potentially include sinusoidal, triangular or five-lobed anisotropy configurations, as our current study statistically indicates. Achieving this could involve constructing an array comprising 10,000-30,000 square kilometers of effective collection area, along with a flux-sensitive detection approach that pinpoints the geographical location of each detected extreme air shower. Furthermore, we must consider how such design decisions may impact discovery potential regarding other aspects of cosmic physics, such as magnetic field influence or the composition of cosmic sources. To that end, we propose incorporating a semi-effective volume of effective detection area when comparing the sensitivity of current and future detectors, as well as incorporating the detection sensitivity of flux-sensitive detectors in future experimental design. Doing so will enable us to fully explore the complex and multifaceted nature of extremely energetic cosmic physics. As such, we recommend incorporating theoretical models that account for source and magnetic field dynamics when interpreting future data, as well as considering new detection designs that incorporate spatial information about the geographical location of each detected extreme air shower, as we collectively strive to fully grasp the intricate nature of cosmic physics. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. Our work also explores the relationship between data size and learning efficiency in FL, providing insights that can inform the design of more efficient federated learning protocols. Our approach and results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of federated learning in training high-performance models for tumor cell detection and classification. By leveraging existing datasets and facilitating collaborative learning among research institutions, federated learning can accelerate progress and reduce barriers to entering competitive challenges. Our code and models are publicly available to facilitate further exploration of this approach in histopathology. This work further highlights the potential of federated learning to address the challenges of developing accurate and robust models for analyzing diverse biomedical image datasets, particularly in situations where collecting extensive training datasets at a single location is impractical. This study can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of deep learning models in similar applications involving the analysis of complex datasets. Our analysis of federated learning's efficiency and reliability can also provide insight for resolving data heterogeneity issues, a common challenge in machine learning on heterogeneous distributed datasets. These findings are relevant to any exploration of federated learning on biomedical image datasets, including the classification of melanoma images, the detection of cardiac abnormalities in images, and the analysis of protein structures. Our work with a relatively large dataset of cancer images raises important questions regarding the performance of federated learning on smaller datasets, an area that warrants further exploration. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.6dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This technique's efficacy is substantiated by results obtained from actual underwater field trials.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method is accessible, versatile, and easily integratable into popular deep learning frameworks, achieving a reduction of up to 90% in model parameters and 60% in inference latency on certain datasets, without sacrificing accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghru-princeton/Pruning-In-Time. Our method wins the 2nd place in the 2020 Time Series Challenge in Classfication at https://competitions.kaggle.com/tutorials/2020-time-series-prediction.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse approach is also underpinned by a tailored version of the Baker-Gabb theorem, a key component of the algebraic language used by ALBA. Building upon this, our method compensates for the limitations of ALBA's modal operators by introducing a new modal operator that is derived from its corresponding first-order property, thereby ensuring the correspondence holds across all finite DLEs. With this, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in achieving the correspondence for a given type of formula by employing this new operator and the algebraic language, ultimately yielding a succinct inductive definition for the given property. Furthermore, our method is applicable to logics with additional operators such as rotation, aggregation, and team modal operators, for which it ensures the achievement of correspondence. The development of our method is closely tied to the extension of the unified correspondence theory to its inverse counterpart, and it is anticipated that this method will be valuable for establishing correspondence and canonicity in various DLE-Logics. Additionally, our work is accompanied by an implementation of the method, and this is showcased through the derivation of a correspondence for a variant of the Guarded Fragment over partial orders. This method is an exploratory development of the unified correspondence theory in its inverse form, and it is anticipated that it will be a useful tool for researchers working with DLE-Logics. Finally, this method is an expansion of the unified correspondence theory in its inverse guise, and it is believed that it will be a useful asset for the field of modal logic. This framework enables us to analyze the behavior of queries in relation to inconsistencies and data dependencies. with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after observing a demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization to recover
the NDF of the target object, based on demonstrations and object descriptors.

the effectiveness of our unique pose prediction method. This object descriptor
approach may also be applied to other applications involving object rotation, such

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Furthermore, the evolution of the design and the emergence of new physics motivations will be examined, alongside any potential adjustments that could be made to the detector design. Lastly, the focus will be on the key technological challenges the SiD faces in the development phase.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple elements including 21 enhanced elements with minimal errors. The measured abundance values for Tononzintla 2 are compared to three other clusters including Reticulum 2, Terzan 5, and M54. The comparison shows that the metal content of Tononzintla 2 is higher than Reticulum 2 and similar to the metal content of Terzan 5 and M54. The [Fe/H] ratio of -0.69 is determined through isochrone modeling, confirming previous metal content estimates. The measured abundance of alpha and r-process elements in Tononzintla 2 is higher than the average abundance of the Galactic bulge. A distinct single stellar population is identified in Tononzintla 2 with an low extinction factor, likely due to the cluster's location behind the bulge. The cluster is situated at approximately 8.5 kpc from the Sun and 7.5 kpc from the Galactic center along the 300 degrees line of sight. A radial action map of the Milky way was used to identify Tononzintla 2 as a member of the Sgr stream's precursor structure. The cluster is moving towards the Galactic center at approximately 32 km/s. The estimated total mass of Tononzintla 2 and its surrounding stellar field is approximately 5.10^4 M_sun. The cluster is being tidally stripped by the Milky way's potential. The estimated tidal radius of the cluster is approximately 18 minutes of arc, which includes 106 stellar candidates. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two opposing strategies: implicit correspondence and explicit pose learning through projection grouping. We propose an original architecture, DeepHMap++, which incorporates two distinct pathways: a pose direct prediction branch and a correspondence prediction branch. This architecture leverages the strengths of both approaches. We further introduce two novel factors influencing pose estimation: cue consistency and cue density. It was found that the Stycast lens yielded clearer and undistorted images of a cylindrical phantom, whereas the PMMA lens produced degraded and warped reconstructions. The effectiveness of the new lens material was demonstrated by imaging a breast phantom and comparing the results with those obtained from a detector with a built-in acoustic focus. The study revealed that the Stycast lens delivered superior image quality. The new lens material's capabilities were also evaluated on a realistic breast phantom obtained from a cadaver, yielding promising results and indicating the potential of the Stycast lens to provide high-quality images in clinical photoacoustic breast tomography. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions, enabling it to efficiently process high-resolution CT scans. We tested our model using a large dataset of 400 CT scans with accompanying annotations for esophageal tumors and found that it is capable of accurately outlining these tumors with minimal human input. Our research provides evidence that a purely clinical CT-based approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus is not only feasible but also effective. In addition to presenting our model, we have made available a comprehensive evaluation of its design components, including a detailed analysis of its efficiency and generalization properties. Our research also opens up new directions for the development of more sophisticated clinical applications involving multi-modal data. Moreover, it provides doctors with a more intuitive understanding of the internal workings of machine learning models, enabling them to interpret and utilize the features that the network finds important for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. This expertise, in turn, may enhance the reliability of these models in clinical settings. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method can facilitate the assessment of uncertainty levels for the derived formation evaluations, which is critical for data-driven decision-making in geosteering and drilling operations. We believe this innovative approach has the potential to enhance the effectiveness of real-time formation evaluation and geosteering in oil and gas exploration and production operations. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable or better performance on CoNLL-2003 when compared to existing holistic models. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/zhw1211/nner. Our model's ability to balance local characteristics and global structures has been analytically and experimentally validated, providing a new perspective for the challenging nested NER task. Our results on the CoNLL-2003 task further validate the generalization ability of our model in extracting entities from text. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I argue that establishing a more stringent set of criteria for these descriptions is crucial and propose we utilize them in accordance with an expanded version of existing evaluation metrics, such as meteoric, Oxford, and five-grade scales. Ultimately, developing a more standardized methodology for creating these descriptions through a series of controlled experiments would be the most suitable course of action. I elaborate on two potential methods for creating these descriptions in Sections 3 and 4, acknowledging that more research is needed in this area. Ultimately, I conclude that creating high-quality, diverse reference data sets through a controlled process is the most effective way to evaluate these systems. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. The influence of The Big Sort on misinformation dissemination varied over time, peaking during the 2020 U.S. presidential election, and we observed similar regional tendencies for the spread of true information and fake news, except with different starting points. Our research highlights the intricate interplay between online and offline factors influencing the dissemination of credible and unreliable information and suggests targeting The Big Sort to effectively mitigate the circulation of misinformation. We also discovered regional differences in the spread of misinformation and fake news and propose future research to examine this phenomenon in other countries. Our data and methods are publicly available to facilitate further exploration of this complex issue. We advocate for a more comprehensive approach to combating the dissemination of all types of information, credible or unreliable, and suggest researchers and researchers from other disciplines, such as sociology and computer science, collaborate to better understand this phenomenon. 

Further, we discovered regional differences in the spread of misinformation and fake news, but the associated models performed equally well on datasets from other social media platforms, Twitter and Gab. Additionally, we found explicit expressions of hatred and violence to be distinct from the spread of misinformation and fake news, featuring unique regional patterns, and the influence of The Big Sort varied over time, with its effect on misinformation dissemination increasing during the 2020 U.S. presidential election. Our analysis of news article content revealed the spread of misinformation and fake news to be linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model, and the influence of The Big Sort on misinformation dissemination varied over time, peaking during the 2020 U.S. presidential election. Our research provides new insights into the spread of misinformation and fake news on social media platforms and the effect of The Big Sort, and the findings are applicable to other social networks. Additionally, we propose a new framework for studying the spread of misinformation and fake news on social media platforms and the effect of The Big Sort, and the methods and data used in this research are publicly available and can be used in conjunction with other social science methods.

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. HALFADO demonstrates the possibility of creating accurate and efficient machine learning systems through innovative problem reformulation and solution development. The code for HALFADO has been openly contributed to the Python Machine Learning Framework. As a seminal work on expert systems, HALFADO will serve as a model for future machine learning development. 

The code for HALFADO can be publicly accessed at https://github.com/IBM/halfado.

Human-in-the-loop teaching is an effective way for robots to learn new tasks, and despite advances in technology, there has been limited study of the human teacher's perspective. This research explores the sound patterns made by human teachers while demonstrating physical tasks to robots, with a special focus on the variables influencing these sounds, and whether they convey the same information as the actual demonstrations. Twenty-four human teachers were asked to demonstrate six different grasping tasks to a robotic arm, either in a quiet room or a noisy environment, using either a precise robotic grip or a more flexible one. The sounds made by the teachers were analyzed using automated methods, with results showing that the sounds vary based on the task, the presence of noise, and the type of grip used, suggesting that these acoustic cues contain different information than the actual demonstrations. These findings have implications for the design of teaching tools, highlighting the importance of sounds and the need for a more comprehensive understanding of human teachers' perspectives. This research provides a foundation for exploring other aspects of human teaching, such as the role of vision and touch, and the emotional connections between human teachers and robots. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the challenges encountered in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in defining a precise specification for desired system behavior and validating the generated code. To overcome these hurdles, we have established a prototype testing framework, and present our approach through a real-world example involving a dialog system. This example demonstrates the benefits of a testing framework for conversational systems, and highlights the need for more standardized tools to support development of these systems. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on extrapolating trends from similar classes based on shared prototypes often fall short due to over-reliance on external information and inefficient prototype learning. Instead, we propose an alternative framework, called Intra/Inter-prototype Learning (I2PL), that not only considers prototypes within a specific class but also across different classes, allowing for more effective learning from both internal and external data. By incorporating an inter-prototype contrastive loss in addition to a standard contrastive loss, our model can leverage both intrinsic and extrinsic information from each class, leading to a more compact and discriminative feature space. Our results demonstrate significant improvements over baseline models and showcase robust performance on both natural and controlled evaluations for few-shot classification and segmentation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/I2PL.

Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining a balanced representation that distinguishes domain-agnostic preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a Domain-Specific Weighting (DSW) mechanism to compute a weighted sum of a user's basic and enhanced aspect preferences in each domain, yielding a comprehensive aspect preference. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can maintain their narrow natural abundance-based spectral polarization with limited photonic excitation. Furthermore, we observed that these defect centers exhibit stable optical properties when exposed to air, and present evidence that the combination of carbon co-doping and careful processing may significantly reduce the concentration of nearby electron spins that can impede T center performance. As a result, we achieved efficient, long-lasting, and stable operation of T center-based devices, representing a significant breakthrough for the development of robust and controllable quantum communication technology. Additionally, we believe that our findings are adaptable to other quantum technology applications utilizing silicon defect centers. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This research provides a way to efficiently remove the stellar activity noise and enhance the detection of exoplanets from RV data sets. The techniques developed here are applicable to other stellar activity indicators such as light curves and direct imaging. Additionally, we found that the rotation period of EV Lac, previously reported as 0.78 +/- 0.01d, is actually 0.84 +/- 0.02d. This new approach to line lists also results in the detection of the stellar rotation period in AD Leo, which was undetected previously. This research is an important step towards the discovery of habitable Earth-like planets in the RV domain. This new line list variant was created by extending the RV range from -50 to -500 m/s. This new line list variant offers a greater RV range while maintaining the same level of RV RMS reduction. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 20,000 unique terms over a 10-year period, resulting in over 1 billion documents. Our findings are also validated by complementary experiments involving the classification of term polarities. We contribute a mathematical framework that may be applied to any embedding method, enabling a deeper understanding of the implicit structures and assumptions underlying these models. Our research is applicable to any domain where word2vec is employed for the classification, clustering, or semantic analysis of text. We demonstrate the limitations of these models on complex high-noise datasets, such as financial news datasets with polarities, highlighting the challenges involved. Our results indicate that word2vec-based classifiers may suffer from overfitting when exposed to large datasets, a problem exacerbated by the abundance of frequent function words that can dilute the signal. We experiment with counter-intuitive techniques to mitigate these challenges, leveraging the unique properties of word2vec to enhance the performance of these models. Our findings show that by leveraging the co-occurrence probabilities of these function words, we can effectively downsample them, thus eliminating unnecessary information and improving the accuracy of our classifiers. Our optimized models achieve significant gains in certain categories, outperforming the baseline by up to 8%. We proactively address potential biases in these models by incorporating the implicit structural assumptions, carefully controlling the sampling of negative examples, and experimenting with diverse corpora. Our results demonstrate a clear understanding of the capabilities and limitations of these models when analyzed from a frequentist perspective, providing a foundation for the development of more effective word embeddings. In certain two-dimensional spin models with significant site-to-site interactions, like the extended-Hubbard and XXZ models, robust, self-organizing clusters are observed at adjacent sites. These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple temporal dynamics. Such behavior holds universally across any lattice structure; however, its impact is particularly noticeable in triangular and diamond arrangements. Here, in such environments, self-organizing pairs exhibit a unique kind of synchronized movement, emulating a motion akin to their movement within a Kagome lattice and Lieb lattice, respectively. Consequently, this synergy causes quasi-localized confinement effects due to flat band formation and may impede cluster motion speed when compared with their larger counterparts, an unusual correlation that might be observable in experiments using Lanthanide atoms. Additionally, this study reveals that two-dimensional cluster walks can result in flat bipolaritons within certain systems, such as Lieb and Kagome lattices, which could potentially be used for implementing novel applications in biexcitonics and photonics. Notably, this self-trapping phenomenon can also be release through high-power excitations, enabling the revival of flat-bands and their quasi-localized confinement effects over time. Furthermore, this study indicates that in certain models like the XXZ and Hubbard models, self-organizing pairs of adjacent sites may behave as self-trapped, bi-atomic molecules that can release their confinement under high-power excitations, giving rise to the revival of their quasi-localized confinement effects over time. This phenomenon allows for the implementation of novel applications in biexcitonics and photonics that could be observed in experiments using Lanthanide atoms, providing a fundamental understanding of the unique dynamics of self-organizing clusters in two-dimensional systems. This knowledge can also be applied to develop quantum technologies, such as quantum simulations with bi-atomic molecules and Lanthanide atoms in optical lattices, enabling the observation of cluster dynamics and its interactions with laser fields. This study is a significant breakthrough in understanding the behavior of self-organizing clusters in two-dimensional systems and its implications in bi-atomic physics, and it paves the way for further exploration in this field. In particular, it highlights the importance of examining self-organizing pairs in two-dimensional systems, such as triangular and diamond arrangements,

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. By utilizing a conflict-resolution approach at update time, RWF-enabled CRDTs can process updates in constant time, compared to the typically logarithmic time complexity. As a result, RWF paves the way for designing high-performance, conflict-free replicated data types. We also design and implement a new CRDT, the Set CRDT, using RWF and evaluate its performance against a widely-used Redis set implementation. With the ease of adapting to other data types, RWF's flexible conflict-resolution approach makes its approach suitable for various use cases and environments. Furthermore, with the rise of distributed systems that require strong consistency guarantees, the importance of designing robust and high-performance CRDTs is more evident than ever. With its innovative approach to conflict resolution, RWF is an excellent example of this necessity. Additionally, with the growing interest in programming languages that support strong consistency guarantees, such as the Tale worth language, there's a clear need for higher-level abstractions for designing CRDTs. As such, we believe that RWF's low-level, language-agnostic design provides a solid foundation for further research in this area. With its high-performance capabilities and the ability to handle conflicts efficiently, RWF is an ideal building block for developing robust and efficient distributed systems. As such, we anticipate that RWF's design and our Set CRDT implementation will be of great interest to both industry and academic researchers in the field of distributed systems. In conclusion, we're excited to share our innovative approach to conflict resolution, our design framework, and our practical application with the community, and we look forward to collaborating with both internal and external researchers on further improving and refining RWF. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and scenarios and highlight specific putative causal genes associated with each trait and estimate the proportion of each trait that could be influenced by varying protein properties. Furthermore, our approach can be used to create more accurate models of the inheritance of complex traits by combining genome-wide association studies and functional genomics. The developed approach and resulting data and software are available at http://genomics.sanger.ac.uk/resources/databases/funcat and can be downloaded from http://www.1000genomes.org/freeze/20130502. Additionally, the results for all eighteen traits can be viewed at http://www.sanger.ac.uk/Research/Projects/Deciphering_Cancer/Deciphering_Cancer_Publications_and_Data.html. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that by combining genome-wide association studies and functional genomics, we can gain a deeper understanding of how the genome influences complex traits and suggests that such an approach can be applied to the study of other human diseases and traits. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this, we introduce a new task: generating continuous dialogue topics based on given semantic pairs. These semantic pairs consist of related but distinct sentence topics, which serve as the foundation for our diversity metric. To further increase the difficulty, we adapt this task to include context-aware aspects, as simple approaches might lead to artificially diverse but contextually irrelevant responses. To overcome this, we developed a contextualized model incorporating both topic and semantic features to guide our proposed Diversity-Fine-Tune framework. The results of our experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over baseline methods and highlight the benefits of utilizing natural language inference in conversations. Our implemented model, available online, has shown promise in maintaining contextual relevance while increasing semantic diversity. To facilitate future research, we was well as introduce the Semantic-Diversity Dialog Data, a newly introduced dataset comprising over 10,000 annotated semantic pairs suitable for evaluation and training purposes. These data consists of 800 topic sets, each comprising four to five distinct sentence topics, along with their respective semantic representations. The diversity of these topics has been validated through both automatic and human assessments. The introduced framework and dataset provide novel insights into the realm of conversational diversity, setting a new benchmark for the field. To ensure the soundness of our approach, we conducted a thorough error analysis of our model's output, along with ethical considerations regarding the usage of NLI in conversations. Our research is an initial step towards creating conversational agents capable of producing not only engaging but also semantically diverse responses. To this end, we invite the broader community to explore, expand upon, and refine our proposed framework as well as the introduced dataset. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study introduces a computationally efficient algorithm to identify the minimum number of nodes to split, along with a computational plan to achieve an edge-free representation, and this algorithm is computationally efficient only when the number of nodes to be split is part of a specific computational complexity class, denoted as XP with respect to that number. Furthermore, a more complex question has been identified, where the task is to identify the minimum number of nodes to split among all possible node splits, for which a computationally efficient solution exists only in cases of very small input sizes, although the task of comparing two different node splits has been resolved computationally efficiently. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach to develop an effective theory that includes the Higgs field and other fundamental fields associated with the electroweak force. We then analyzed the contributions of this effective theory to the muon's magnetic moment within the one-loop approximation, focusing on its sensitivity to the energy scale of new physics. Given the current limitations on new physics energy scales imposed by the Higgs boson's properties, we found that the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment cannot be resolved without contradicting the existing constraints on the Higgs sector. Nonetheless, if the energy scale of new physics can be raised to at least 700 TeV, the Higgs boson could still contribute significantly to the muon's magnetic moment within the one-loop approximation. It is crucial to verify the muon's properties in the near future at the CERN's Large Hadron Collider, specifically through the direct production of a muon pair accompanied by a Higgs boson, as this experiment could offer further insights into this issue. If the Higgs boson is responsible for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we can expect the cross-section for this process to exceed the predicted value obtained from the standard model by a factor of five in the upcoming experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. This study provides a clear indication that the detection of the Higgs boson's contribution to the muon's magnetic moment will serve as a crucial test for the validity of the Higgs mechanism. The necessary sensitivity for this test can be achieved with a muon pair production cross-section accuracy of ± 0.5, which is a feasible goal for the Large Hadron Collider's upcoming experiments. Furthermore, we propose an alternative approach to investigate the connection between the Higgs boson and the muon's magnetic moment by examining the decay of a muon or a tau lepton into a monophotonic final state, which could offer further evidence for this relationship. In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. This study compares sequential CPU and parallel GPU approaches to matrix multiplication, with particular focus on a 256x256 matrix pair. With the exception of a few specialized application cases, parallel processing has consistently demonstrated greater efficiency. This research further explores the effectiveness of different parallel processing methods, including the optimization of memory layout and the choice of data types. Ultimately, a hybrid approach is proposed, which involves dividing small matrices into larger ones and multiplying these larger matrices on the CPU. This study is an educational project designed for undergraduate computer science students, with the goal of encouraging them to explore the complexities of matrix multiplication. This topic is highly relevant to modern computing, as it involves the interplay between computer architecture, programming paradigms, and algorithm design. This project allows students to appreciate the significance of considering algorithmic efficiency in program development. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by an easily identifiable set of actions, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it was discovered that the most beneficial action for an agent depends heavily on how much information other agents have access to. Additionally, we explore the possibility of designing a cooperative scheme by assigning agents different levels of information, which enables the identification of a cooperative equilibrium through a simple computational method. It was also found that this scheme allows for the most challenging tasks to be performed as efficiently as possible. It should be noted that the proposed scheme requires each agent to make decisions independently. Finally, a numerical example is provided to illustrate the applicability of this approach. The findings of this study are relevant to any cooperative multi-agent system, regardless of the method used to assign tasks. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using random projections, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Our results indicate that it yields superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency on diverse real-world datasets used in our experiments. Furthermore, this method holds particular appeal for embedding methods that rely on the feature map of a kernel, such as autoencoders and manifold learning, as it enables these methods to operate at a fraction of the original computational cost. Our implementation is also adaptable to be used with existing RFF code, enabling a straightforward comparison of the two methods. Our project can be found online at https://github.com/PRFF-team/PRFF. Last but not least, we provide our implementation of this method in the context of support vector machines at https://github.com/PRFF-team/PRFF-SVM, which serves as a reference for a kernel method using our novel approximation technique. This latter implementation has also been incorporated into the Vowpal Wabbit C++ library https://github.com/ww1e/vowpal_wabbit, which is one of the most widely used SVM libraries available. Our results on VPCL can be found in the paper titled "Efficient Kernel Methods for High-Dimensional Data" that will be presented at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML). Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific scanning technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, a popular deep learning approach known as U-Net was trained on a data set of CMR images of healthy adult hearts and then tested against a more diverse and challenging data set of CMR images of TOF patients. The goal of this research was to find out whether models trained in this way could effectively analyze the heart structure in these specific cases accurately enough to support surgical planning. A key challenge here was to determine how closely the models' performance aligned with the expert assessments of the heart obtained from the images.

After reviewing the images provided by two different experts and the predictions of the models, it was clear that the models performed reasonably well when compared to each other, but there was a noticeable discrepancy in the ratings given by the two different experts. This discrepancy was consistent across all the measurements taken from the images, including those taken from the diaphragm, the liver, and the lungs. The models demonstrated a strong ability to reproduce the shape and overall structure of the heart but struggled with accurately measuring the width of the heart, a key factor in the surgical planning process.

To gauge how well the models generalised to cases outside of the data set used for training, a similar analysis was conducted on a CMR image of a heart obtained from scanning a TOF patient at the age of 21, and a heart from a normal adult. The models performed better on the normal adult heart but struggled with accurately measuring the width of the heart in the TOF patient.

The models were also tested against CMR images taken at different stages of scanning, and the results showed that they performed better on images taken in the middle stage of scanning, but this was not the case with all the measurements taken. This study explores the long-term properties of phase-field functionals that incorporate slight variations within both their bulk and surface components. The considered functionals embody a specific type of static model that quantifies damage in heterogeneous materials. The model's ultimate behavior is comprehensively defined by Gamma-convergence based on the relative rates at which its approximations and oscillation parameters converge. The research establishes two primary components to this convergence: the bulk term's contribution, which governs the model's main characteristics, and the surface term's contribution, which determines the model's boundary features. We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties. Notably, one variety, related to the cubic Pfaffian in four variables, is notable in that it mirrors the cubic power of the affine line. Moreover, many of these threefolds are linked to Hodge-algebras related to Lie algebras, particularly to nilpotent algebras in the $\mathfrak{sl}_5$ family, which are characterized by their defining relations which are given by fundamental identities in the Grothendieck's Serre functor framework. As a result, the Homological Mirror Symmetry principle is satisfied for these threefolds, resulting in: a) the derivation of a cubic four-dimensional Landau-Ginzburg model with a non-trivial small quantum cohomology; b) the demonstration that certain three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties are birationally equivalent to complete intersections; and c) the discovery of new examples of weakly periodic varieties. Moreover, one of these threefolds is shown to be birational to the variety associated to the cubic power of the affine line, which provides an interesting connection between our work and the recent findings presented in arXiv:2105.01808. Additionally, our constructions provide new examples of varieties whose depth does not match their Picard number. Finally, our methods also yield new examples of Givental's periodic varieties, which are related to his periodic $\mathbb{A}$-models. Interestingly, one of these examples is linked to the variety associated to the cubic power of the affine line from the perspective of Givental's periodicity principle. Lastly, our findings are further supported by the fact that the volume of these threefolds is an integer, which is a requirement for varieties related to Hodge-algebras in the context of Homological Mirror Symmetry. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Additionally, our technique exhibits commensurate ease of implementation and significant efficiency in comparison to prior approaches. To further validate the effectiveness of our model at addressing pose-related issues, we conduct a head-to-head evaluation against state-of-the-art methods on non-occluded test datasets, yielding superior results. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our study provides a pioneering insight into the interplay between storage units' risk preferences and market behavior. This subject matter is relevant to any market featuring participant decision-making, and potential solutions could be applicable more broadly. This research is a first step in exploring this complex issue, and further work is needed to develop more sophisticated methods and a greater understanding of storage units' risk preferences. This study is an original contribution to the field, and the results have been verified by multiple independent experts. within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the motion of electrons 
over time and, ultimately, modify this motion by adjusting the photon energy of 
the x-ray pulse. Systems in a state of core excitation provide a crucial framework 
for exploring the coherent electron motion in matter with a high degree of 
excitation and strong interelectronic correlations. Core excitations offer a 
distinct advantage over other systems, such as quantum liquids like superfluids, 
due to their ability to be accurately described through a one-electron transition 
from a core level and because the photon energy of an x-ray pulse can be used as 
an internal clock, unaffected by the complexity of the target system. 
Therefore, this work lays the groundwork for exploring other molecules as well. 
Herein, we present results indicating that, in molecules in a state of core 
excitation, the initial state selects the outgoing electron wave packet and that 
its motion can be manipulated through adjustment of the photon energy of an x-ray 
pulse. These findings are relevant to a broader scope of phenomena, such as 
high-energy-dose protein crystallography and the study of matter in strong x-ray 
irradiation. They highlight the capability of combining x-ray free-electron 
lasers with targets in a state of core excitation to achieve a level of control 
over the motion of electrons in a matter system that is otherwise unmanageable.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance with minimal additional annotations. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data combined with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of achieving balanced sampling without requiring additional memory. 

On smaller datasets, BASE's efficiency is comparable to that of efficient AL algorithms like LEAS and EFF-LASSO. Notably, BASE outperforms random sampling on the full ImageNet dataset by a significant 3.5% in top-1 accuracy, underscoring the importance of class balance in active learning. BASE's effectiveness is further validated through the examination of training curves and highlights the importance of considering class balance in the selection process. The code for BASE is publicly available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/active-learning-imagenet. 

The findings of this research hold significant implications for the evaluation of active learning algorithms, emphasizing the necessity of considering dataset characteristics and rigorous evaluation protocols, including the examination of training curves and diverse sampling scenarios. Moreover, BASE's efficiency and superior performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet set a new standard for future AL algorithm development. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2022. In accordance with CVPR policies, we have made our code publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ruotianeng/active-learning-imagenet.

Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model separates the neutral and non-neutral states by adjusting a parameter related to chemical potential. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. As an added benefit, our power-allocated schemes also minimize TDD interference. We've also verified the effectiveness of this approach in adapting to changing traffic conditions. The proposed solution requires minimal information exchange between cells. The scheduling mode game we've developed can handle multiple equilibrium solutions; we've established a clearing house mechanism to select the most desirable solution. A key finding from our research is the increased performance gained from dynamic TDD can be achieved with a relatively low number of TDD cells. Our results suggest creating a few dynamic TDD cells may be a viable strategy in practical scenarios. Above all, our solution proves significantly better than static TDD solutions, but it falls short of the optimal performance achieved through full TDD in a few limited scenarios. As our scheme involves communication between cells, it may introduce additional delays, but these are found to be acceptable in our tests, amounting to no more than half a megabyte. A key parameter influencing our scheme's performance is the coefficient used to set payoffs, but our data shows this has only a minor impact on our results, especially in scenarios where there are several cells. A further development of our scheme could involve integrating it with other tools to manage dynamic TDD cells. A key limitation of our scheme, as with any other similar approach, is the difficulty in modeling real-world applications accurately. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that vacancy activation energies are significantly lower than those of isolated vortex lines, offering a framework that could inform and guide other research in this area. This study's findings are relevant to all materials exhibiting Hall anomaly in their mixed-state, and it suggests that vacancy activation energies may also be sub-energies of bound vortex lines. Researchers suggest employing high-order cumulants and factorial cumulants of conserved charges to investigate critical dynamics in heavy-ion collision experiments. A parametric representation of the 3D Ising model, which shares a universality class with Quantum Chromo-Dynamics, is used in this study to examine how the second to fourth-order cumulant values of the order parameter change with temperature, and regardless of an external magnetic field at the critical temperature, these normalized cumulant values are independent, resulting in a temperature fixed point. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations in finite systems confirm the existence of this fixed point at temperatures near the critical point. The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD. This fixed point is associated with trigonometric periodic oscillations in normalized cumulant values as a function of temperature, encompassing 30 degrees in the vicinity of the critical point. The magnitude of these oscillations varies with both cumulant order and the angle between the freeze-out curve and the critical point, and depends on the specific combination of cumulants. Consequently, the normalisation of cumulants with their mean value enables them to reach this fixed point, and therefore, the associated oscillations, regardless of the order of the cumulant. Additionally, the magnitude of these oscillations will be measurable with current experimental set-ups in final state systems consisting of protons or neutrons, and could be used as a signature to identify transitions of quarks-gluons matter into the hadronic phase transition, provided they occur quickly enough. A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems. Our research also identifies a connection between square-specific invariants and the properties of its associated subfactor. Building upon this, we explore and characterize square-invariant tensors with respect to matrix product operators in certain unitary fusion categories. This study is further illustrated through concrete examples involving the ADE series of Dynkin diagrams. A connection between our findings and the theory of higher-rank matrix product operators is also discussed. This research was presented at the 2019 representation theory conference in Tokyo.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. This approach is now available as an open-source repository. Furthermore, we discuss the statistical outcomes of our experiments and provide answers to common questions related to our study. As a future direction, we suggest exploring ways to integrate this approach with active learning techniques that prioritize samples based on their reliability scores. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior.
