The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, data augmentation techniques have proven beneficial for both NLP and computer vision tasks.  Building upon these concepts, this paper introduces a novel data augmentation method called Context-gloss augmentation, which leverages knowledge from bilingual dictionaries to add context-gloss pairs to existing datasets, thereby promoting the development of multiple sense embeddings for polysemous words.  Experiments conducted on the SENSEVAL dataset demonstrate that Context-gloss augmentation yields superior performance when compared to baseline models and other data augmentation methods.  Moreover, this proposed method is cost-effective and efficient in tailoring the training process to account for polysemous words with multiple senses.  Further analysis of the results indicates that Context-gloss augmentation not only enhances the performance on the target task but also promotes the development of more interpretable word embeddings.  These findings are corroborated by additional experiments conducted on the GLUE dataset, which reveal that words with low lexical entailment scores tend to have multiple sense embeddings.  Consequently, words with high lexical entailment scores typically have fewer sense embeddings.  Ultimately, this paper's proposed Context-gloss augmentation method offers a versatile and effective approach for addressing the limitations of single-best predictions in NLP tasks. In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the equipped vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. When the search algorithm's population size matches the number of road design parameters, this results in the optimal balance between speedy testing and practicality. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. The findings presented in this paper provide a foundation for further exploration into the application of IRS technology in radar systems. We propose the term 'IRS-Aided Radar' (IAR) to describe systems utilizing IRS technology and outline potential research directions for future study. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of various residual reflections from the IRS on the received radar signals, acknowledging their influence as a form of coherent noise. The results indicate target parameter estimation performance degradations when comparing optimized and non-optimized scenarios, with a relative strength of $~10^{-2}$ in terms of the former's accuracy when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. The findings presented in this paper provide a foundation for further exploration into the application of IRS technology in radar systems. We propose the term 'IRS-Aided Radar' (IAR) to describe systems utilizing IRS technology and outline potential research directions for future study. The numerical simulations and analyses conducted in this paper also raise implications for the design of IRS configurations in radar applications. With the aim of enhancing target parameter estimation performance, we examine the effects of varying IRS sizes, locations, and electrical properties. The results indicate these factors significantly influence the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation and, by extension, the overall performance of IAR systems. The findings presented in this paper provide a foundation for further exploration into the application of IRS technology in radar systems.

Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect mutations in only a small percentage, but this outcome serves as a motivation for future research to address (1) the enhancement of fuzzer performance in detecting sophisticated failures and (2) the development of more effective techniques for triggering mutations and faults. In addition to presenting evaluation results, this paper provides guidance to researchers and practitioners on the selection of suitable mutations and the assessment of fuzzer performance. This evaluation framework is available online for anyone to utilize and expand upon. Triggering mutations is proposed as a new metric for evaluating fuzzers, and a discussion on the advantages of combining traditional and modern mutation analysis methods is presented. This paper is an expansion of our previous work presented at the 2019 International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis. Additionally, this paper has been accepted for presentation at the 2023 International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.6% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. In addition, our NMC showed robust performance on unseen classes in the CoRe 50 benchmark, achieving 62.1% overall accuracy, surpassing the performance of many contemporary continual learning techniques. These findings suggest that the use of complex models in continual learning may not be necessary and that a simple baseline with a frozen pre-trained model can effectively address the challenges of continual learning in the image domain. In particular, this study highlights the efficacy of self-synchronization via a frozen representation, and this may have implications for continual learning in other domains and with label information. Human evaluation of our NMC's decision-making process revealed interesting insights into its strengths and weaknesses, providing a framework for the continued development of simple yet effective continual learning methods. In addition, our results indicate that the performance of our NMC can be further enhanced by implementing a rehearsal buffer with our Nearest Mean Classifier, resulting in improved accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark. In this case, our efficient and effective rehearsal buffer strategy achieved 92.5% accuracy on this benchmark, surpassing the performance of many contemporary continual learning techniques. In conclusion, this study successfully challenged the necessity of complex models utilizing pre-trained transformers in continual learning and demonstrated the efficacy of simple alternatives in comparison. Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. Typically, in Ni isotopes, a collective 2+ state is found at much higher energies, far beyond 3500 keV. This breakthrough was further supported by Monte Carlo shell model results, which demonstrated that both the 0+ and 2+ states shared similar configurations, in contrast to the usual separation seen in other Ni isotopes. Additionally, a study using the tensor monopole interaction helped to drive this unique, two-state shape coexistence phenomenon. This interaction is known to contribute significantly to the formation of T=2 pair correlations, and it was found to play a crucial role in 64Ni, where it caused the 0+ and 2+ states to coexist, a phenomenon that had far-reaching implications for understanding other low-spin states in this nucleus. Furthermore, this research indicated that the combination of pair correlations and the monopole tensor interaction led to a quasi-unstable situation in 64Ni, where small changes could result in either a prolate or an oblate shape dominating, and thus, this study has significant implications for theoretical models, and highlights the importance of considering multi-body interactions in shell model studies.

We examine whether approximately optimal mixed strategies can be identified by observing actions resulting from random mixed strategies in independent plays of a Lipschitz game with a large number of players. Specifically, we investigate how the number of necessary independent experiments varies with respect to key parameters of the game. We find that, in a class of convex games subject to specific payoff constraints, approximately optimal mixed strategies can be accurately identified with a finite number of independent experiments, independent of the game's dimensionality. On the other hand, in a class of nonconvex games with smoothly bounded payoff functions, approximately optimal mixed strategies may not be accurately identified even with an infinitely large number of independent experiments, depending on the game's dimensionality. This finding is significant because it shows that recent advances in finding equilibria in online learning settings may not translate to similar efficiency in query complexity. We also introduce a new lower bound method that builds on existing approaches and provides a simple proof strategy for lower bound results in online learning settings. This method measures the complexity of an online learning problem by considering the minimum distance between any two distinct mixed strategies, characterized by their payoff differences under smooth constraints. This method can be applied to a broader class of games than previous approaches, enabling the derivation of more general lower bound results. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by deriving new lower bounds for various online learning problems, including a problem previously solved by Aggarwal et al. (2013) and several problems with multiple action spaces. Additionally, we use this method to establish lower bounds for offline approximation, a problem previously solved by Daskalakis et al. (2013) and others. This method can be viewed as an extension of the variance-based lower bounds used in offline approximation, and it provides a new perspective on the study of online approximation. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, especially in high-dimensional settings like NLP, where the risk of overfitting is elevated. A commonly employed t-statistic or similar adjustment may not adequately account for this issue, as it primarily targets reducing bias error. Given the inherent difficulty of estimating performance differences directly, we suggest employing the Jensen-Shannon divergence as a variance-reducing strategy in parameter tuning. This approach is less prone to the instabilities associated with grid search or Bayesian optimization, as it encourages exploration of the parameter space based on a measure of similarity rather than a fixed structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to several NLP tasks involving text classification, where it yields improved performance compared to standard techniques. Additionally, we investigate the applicability of this approach to other machine learning tasks beyond NLP. The implementation of this approach is available as part of the HyperTuneCV module for Python. Furthermore, we investigate the role of model selection, examining whether our proposed approach is effective in identifying the optimal model for a given task. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. This study supplements the existing 2-dimensional event classification for WIMP interactions with nuclei by introducing new variables, including the velocity of the WIMP, the scattering angle, and their combination. Utilizing a detailed 3-dimensional galactic rotation velocity field for the Milky Way, we have generated a comprehensive set of local nucleon velocities. Our research reveals the inherent velocity-recoil angle structure for WIMP interactions and demonstrates how the velocity-recoil angle correlation changes across various dark matter densities. Additionally, our findings encompass a wide range of dark matter candidates, encompassing the lightest possible singlet scalar, gaugino, Higgsino, and fermion masses spanning from 12 to 700 GeV. Our work is applicable to the broad spectrum of dark matter models and is pertinent to present-day dark matter densities. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. Ultimately, all-assembled datasets along with the research on the container crisis data are offered for academic researchers to explore further. 

For the first time in academic research, the following six essential time series for the container shipping industry have been comprehensively quantified from 1966 to 2009: (i) world shipping quantity (WSQ), (ii) total worldwide freight revenue (TFFR), (iii) new ship prices (NSP), (iv) used ship prices (USP), and (v) scrap ship prices (SSP). With regard to WSQ, a top-down approach has been employed using the most up-to-date information available from the World Shipping Council, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, and the Containerisation International annual yearbooks. For the purpose of validating the datasets, a shipping quantity model has been developed using the knowledge of shipping industry experts and former top executives. This model has been tested from 1966 to 1980 and verified from 1981 to 2009. 

In the 1980s, the container shipping industry experienced a significant shift in market dynamics due to the dissolution of shipping monopolies. To examine these changes, a time series analysis was conducted to identify structural changes in the data variables. According to the findings, the dissolution of shipping monopolies led to a decrease in the volatility of shipping quantities and freight rates. Additionally, used ship prices began to converge towards new ship prices, and the gap between used and scrap ship prices narrowed. Furthermore, the ratio of used ship prices to new ship prices decreased over time as the industry transitioned from a monopolistic to a competitive market structure.

This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as an penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower equipment costs because certain devices are no longer necessary. The PPC algorithm is mathematically analyzed, and it is demonstrated that it converges to the optimal solution under specified conditions. The proposed algorithm is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior performance compared to traditional approaches. The code is publicly available online. The proposed algorithm achieves notable improvements in energy costs, device costs, and social welfare in a case study involving over 5000 electric vehicles across three days. The study reveals a significant 50% reduction in communication requirements and a 90% decrease in variable counts, resulting in energy cost savings of up to $1043, device cost savings of up to $1043, and increased social welfare by up to $2066. The study also examines the impact of different encoder architectures on MEF and finds that a simpler architecture can lead to energy savings of up to $533, device savings of up to $533, and welfare gains of up to $1066. The research demonstrates the MEF-PPC framework's effectiveness and identifies areas for further research, including the development of more robust and distributed online optimization approaches, especially for larger-scale applications involving numerous electric vehicles. The study's findings and results provide a foundation for tackling a wide range of real-time control challenges arising from the efficient management of controllable loads. The issue of aggregate flexibility hinges on the strategic deployment of controllable loads to minimize costs, with a feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback, and an algorithm called penalized predictive control, both of which are novel contributions to this field. The proposed study is a landmark work for the department author, and as the second paper, it marks an expansion of research scope

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, identifying star formation rates and gas outflow velocities across 10-kiloparsec areas around the galaxy's center. Our analysis indicates a larger outflow velocity where star formation occurs more rapidly, supporting the hypothesis that feedback from galaxy outflows suppress star formation. This relationship is reflected in the DUVET model, predicting the effect of gas outflows on the regulation of star formation. However, our data also shows the impact of gas accretion on this process, revealing a more complex interplay between star formation, galaxy outflows, and gas supply, influenced by the galaxy's rotation curve and potential energy. As a result, the DUVET model only partially accounts for the observed relationship between star formation and outflow velocity. 

Additionally, we found evidence for the collapse of gas streams as potential sites of high-efficiency star formation, along with enhanced outflow velocities. These star-forming regions exhibit different properties compared to the more typical quiescent areas of the galaxy. Furthermore, by analyzing the galaxy's molecular gas distribution, we identified a greater total mass of gas involved in galaxy outflows than initially estimated, along with evidence for the enrichment of gas outflows with heavy elements. These enriched outflows can potentially contribute to the formation of metal-poor galaxies. 

Our observations further reveal a greater rotation curve in the outer galaxy regions, along with a greater potential energy difference at the transition from star-forming to quiescent areas, both of which influence the galaxy's behavior. A more detailed analysis of these factors is essential to fully understand the galactic outflows and the regulation of star formation in this galaxy. 

Our study provides a better comprehension of the interplay between star formation, galaxy outflows, and gas supply, with implications for the DUVET model, and highlights the importance of observing galactic outflows over larger spatial areas around the galaxy's center. 

Finally, by analyzing the galaxy's properties, we found it to be an analog of a local starburst galaxy, specifically Mrk 311. Observations of this galaxy are consistent with those of our study, along with predictions made by the DUVET model. 

Sptizers far-infrared observations of this galaxy, however, indicate a greater far-infrared luminosity, along with a greater star formation rate and a greater galactic outflow velocity. However, the DUVET model still predicts a positive correlation between far-infrared luminosity and outflow velocity.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  With DistQualityAssessment, users can now perform a wider range of quality assessments on very large-scale Linked Data collections, thereby unlocking their full potential for other analytics tasks.  This project has been hosted on GitHub under https://github.com/CSA-UK/DistQualityAssessment, and the detailed technical details are available to download from http://hdl.handle.net/10380/5147.  This work is also presented at the 11th International Conference on Natural Computing, 2019.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. These findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the existence of gas outflows in active galaxies. They also highlight the importance of considering multiple processes such as photoionization, shocks, and mass flows in interpreting the ionization states of active galaxies. Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 exhibit outflow temperatures comparable to those found in ultra-luminous active galaxies, while Mrk 607's mass flows are significantly less powerful. The power of these outflows, estimated by total ionizing power and shock energy, range from 0.3 to 3 barries. These outcomes add to previous research identifying gas outflows in active galaxies, and Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 are the third and fourth examples of objects where the axis of these outflows is observed to be perpendicular to ionization axes.

As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by executing numerous virtual devices in parallel, and enables developers to define complex scenarios through simple scripts based on the Petri Net model. The effectiveness of Frisbee was confirmed through a use case involving the development of an intelligent traffic system. Frisbee's development also paves the way for the creation of more advanced testing techniques, such as concolic testing and symbolic execution, which have previously been unexplored in the context of IoT. With Frisbee, developers can now tackle complex IoT projects with greater confidence. The framework's source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license on GitHub, and it has been showcased at the Edge Computing Workshop hosted by the IEEE in 2021. Further details can be found in the ICSME 2021 conference proceedings. Building upon Frisbee's success, we have created an open-source competition, Frisbee Challenge, which aims to evaluate the testing capabilities of Edge IoT applications. The challenge's details have been posted on the Artifact Evaluation website for the 2022 edition of the ACM/SPEC International Conference on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement. The Frisbee Challenge has sparked interest from top research institutions and industrial companies, which has inspired us to release Frisbee's source code as an open-source baseline for the evaluation of IOT testbeds. The code is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. Our approach achieved a 25% gain in mean average precision at a strict threshold on the far-field validation dataset. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Additionally, we observed a distinct soft X-ray spectrum during the high flux phase, which differs significantly from the rest of the decline phase, characterized by a power law index of 0.26 and no notable spectral features. Moreover, we detected no notable breaks in power law spectra across the decline phase, not even at the e-folding energy of 10 keV, which is an uncommon finding among X-ray pulsars. Our detection of a mHz QPO and a Cyclotron Line in IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst adds another member to the growing list of low frequency Pulsar Oscillations, while also highlighting the unique spectral characteristics of this intermediate spin binary system.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. To address this, we introduce the concept of a "cheap" super-sampler, an inexpensive method to generate additional data for challenging evaluation tasks based on easy tasks, which, in turn, enables the efficient training of models for these evaluation tasks. Eventually, our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in enhancing the performance of models on evaluation tasks over their baseline counterparts. Furthermore, we observe the efficacy of this approach across multiple evaluation tasks and discover the surprising outcome that some evaluation tasks prove more amenable to optimization than others and that the optimized models exhibit distinct characteristics that reflect their performance on each task. Lastly, we explore the applicability of this approach to other generative text generation tasks. In conclusion, this work underscores the significance of scrutinizing the internal representations used in generative text generation models and offers novel methods for evaluating and enhancing the performance of these representations. Additionally, the proposed approach proves useful in addressing the challenging issue of optimizing time-aware dialogue models. With considerable potential, future research could further explore the implications of our findings across multiple domains and datasets and the potential for our approach to be adapted for models involving multiple encoders and decoders. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we establish lower limits on the mass of ultra-light gravitons, placing them above $2.3\times 10^{-20}$eV, and upper limits on the mass of ultra-light Kaluza-Klein gravitons, assuming their existence could prevent the non-observation of black hole emptying. This research paves the way for the investigation of other ultra-light multi-dimensionally inspired particles.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. Furthermore, we outline various research opportunities for Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory, emphasizing its potential for supernova detection, monitoring water layers, and facilitating cosmogenic neutrino studies. SBN ( Aberdeen Tunnel's Neutrino Detector) is the name given to this apparatus, with its data accessible through the arXiv repository at https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07834 for further reference. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the TESS Full Pixel Data, suitable for follow-up observations with high precision. These targets are representative of the most commonly found exoplanets in the catalog, excluding those discovered with the radial action principle. Furthermore, the survey will explore how various physical properties of planets, either host stars or planetary systems, are linked to each other. The target selection strategy is transparent and open-source, which can be applied to any similar ground-based follow-up study of transit planets. The survey will continue to incorporate new data from the TESS Mission and is accessible at http://pragel.brown.edu:8080/teks/. The target list for the 100 allocated Keck/HIRES nights includes 39 systems featuring multiple planets, 36 systems with planets orbiting solar-type stars, and 14 systems featuring planets that are suitable for study with the JWST. The survey is also exploring the potential for discovering new planets through the analysis of activity indicators, as well as the detection of planets that exhibit tidal synchronization or orbital obliquity. The survey's targets with detectable planet transits are listed on the exoplanet archive under "TEKS". The oversight committee for the NSF's Telescope System Instrumentation Package Early Science Program approved the proposal, and the survey is now utilizing the Keck/HIRES and TESS Full Pixel Data via the telescope's data system, TDN. Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  To validate the system's effectiveness in detecting fraud, a set of 20 ID cards with known fraud statuses were analyzed.  When tested against these samples, the system accurately identified all valid ID cards but failed to detect two out of three fake ID cards.  To further improve the system's ability to detect fake ID cards, it is recommended to incorporate Machine Learning algorithms capable of analyzing the text and image components of ID cards simultaneously.  The system's ID card extraction tool, IDCT, is available for download at https://drive.google.com/file/d/2BieYJQdJ7j0jQgDqDNiY4sO5bI7RjXgC/edit.  The system's source code, meanwhile, can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/AndrianKurniawan/IDCardExtractor.  This project offers numerous takeaways for undergraduate students enrolled in the ID card extraction course, particularly takeaways on ID card extraction, OCR, and NLP.  Additionally, this project is an excellent example for graduate students seeking research topics, specifically research topics on ID card extraction, OCR, and NLP. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. A new approach to analyzing spin state data was also introduced, where the phase shift is represented as a quadratic function rather than an exponential curve, which led to a greater understanding of the YORP acceleration in rotation rates. Additionally, this new method can also identify potential variations in the shape and rotation characteristics of these small asteroids. As the light curve observations for these asteroids are expected to show a phase shift greater than the detection limit in the near future, further analysis of their data using this new approach is expected to provide valuable insights into the effects of the Yarkovsky and Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effects on rotation rates and shapes.

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Furthermore, we identified clusters of users who consistently interacted with each other, with some communities attracting the attention of the original poster more frequently than others. Our analysis also revealed inequalities in online discussions, with some users contributing more than others, and also shedding light on user behavior, such as commenting on posts from politicians but not engaging with comments from those politicians. Lastly, we explored community characteristics and observed that certain features, such as comment length and the prevalence of emojis and hashtags, varied across communities, with some communities exhibiting more negative language. Furthermore, we discovered that some users possessed a unique ability to initiate discussions and draw in other commenters, while also influencing the tone of the discussion. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Additionally, this applies to homeomorphisms of the plane and Riemannian manifolds of non-positive curvature. This finding contradicts previous assumptions regarding the topological properties of certain groups. Our proof relies on extending a permutation-based argument initially developed by the second author for homeomorphisms of the plane, as well as recent developments related to Loeb spaces and their associated dynamics. Furthermore, this leads to implications regarding the compactness of certain subgroups within the context of compact-open topology. Lastly, we explore potential connections between these findings and the principles of compactness, discussing relevant open questions. Our approach also yields a new, compact-open topology-based interpretation of the concept of relatively compact action. This, in turn, raises questions regarding the relationship between this notion and the more established standard of relatively compact action. Finally, we establish that certain groups with relatively compact action do not possess topological compactness when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This includes groups such as homeomorphisms of the plane with a specific transitivity level and groups with non-positive curvature in higher-dimensional manifolds. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or be associated with the Local Association. Using the field MUSS stars as examples, the researchers verified the validity and applicability of their new approach. The method and the sample described in this study will facilitate future research on the internal structure of M-dwarfs and any detected transits or radial velocity variations. The developed approach and the MUSS database are open to the scientific community to facilitate further exploration of these low-mass stars. The new framework and the MUSS targets are also expected to contribute to the improvement of computer modeling of M-dwarfs. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
Experiments confirmed the existence of line waves at both 0.5 and 1.5 THz, and numerical modeling showed their potential to produce extremely small mode size, polarization-based beam steering, and enhanced local fields, which could be applied in enhanced optical sensing and other areas.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis
network's periodic elements. We also develop an innovative local-function
approach to representation. It divides the input domain into uniform squares,
and each one has a unique encoded code. Then, at inference time, a highly
realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning
or inferring the entire codebook. Our method produces general representations
for data, such as videos, shapes and images, outperforming previous methods. We
also show that our approach is highly flexible, enabling the easy creation
of custom codebooks and networks. Our results show our method produces high
quality, general representations of data across various types and applications
like video, 3D shapes and images, and that it compares favorably to state-of-
the-art techniques like Fourier Neural Operators, Sine-Wave Normalizing Flows
and Positional Encodings, and that our method is versatile, allowing the
easy creation of custom codebooks and networks from scratch. Our method is
also tested on real-world videos and images, and it produces high-quality,
general representations of data across various types and applications. Our code
and experiments are available at https://github.com/anderson-bittar/modulated
periodic-activations. Our method outperforms previous methods on data
representation tasks, and it is available online at https://anderson-bittar.com
projects/modulated-periodic-activations. It was nominated for the ICLR 2023
Travel Award. Our method was also featured in an interview with the MIT CSAIL
Director, Professor Tommer Schwartz, on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch
?v=QG6s5jTj5QY. Our method was selected for an oral presentation at the 35th

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, our data highlight the critical role that perception of social agency plays in shaping the animacy spectrum, a concept that has implications for hispanized theories of how we process biological entities. Additionally, our evidence supports the idea that the presence of animal-like visual features is necessary but not sufficient on its own to explain the presence of agency in non-animal objects, a finding that has bearing on our comprehension of the concept of animacy in the mesial fusiform gyrus. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. The modified logic, which we call QREHL, allows the quantification of pre-/postconditions using "expectations," in addition to the original "relations." We have demonstrated that QREHL is effective in deriving validities for quantum programming languages with additional features, including loops with a dependency on history and input/output operations defined by relations and expectations. Furthermore, QREHL has been proven to be at least as expressive as Hoare logic with relations and preconditions in classical programming. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic filling factor. The results suggest that the bias originates primarily from the bias inherent to the continuum intensity map rather than the inversion algorithm. To mitigate this, a straightforward correction was proposed; however, it ultimately proved insufficient. Consequently, a more complex approach involving the filling factor was explored but encountered difficulties in convergence. Ultimately, a straightforward yet effective solution was found, involving a simple correction to the chi-squared statistic in the optimization algorithm. This technique successfully minimizes the bias below the level of noise in the observations. The authors also investigate the effects of bias on the estimation of other map parameters and corresponding quantities like polar flux, magnetic energy, and net horizontal fields. The proposed correction method is tested on additional inverse problems, demonstrating its generality and utility. This study's findings are relevant to all inversion algorithms that rely on the Grad-Rentov scheme and can serve as a model for analyzing and addressing similar bias issues in other inverse problems. The authors' solution, along with relevant modifications to the optimization algorithm, is available upon request. The study's results are primarily based on the CHAOS-2 potential field model and the ASEP inversion code, both developed by the University of Del Plano. The provided data and modified code can be accessed through the GitHub repository https://github.com/awenger/SEP-inversionbias, along with the authors' contact information. The provided data encompasses full-resolution vector magnetic field maps derived from the SDO/HELIO for the active region NOAA 11659, obtained on 2017 April 18 at 11:00 UT. The derived data, including the proposed correction method and modified ASEP code, can be found at https://doi.org/10.20399/nasavc_0001_0001. A comprehensive analysis of 301 young star clusters in 31 galaxies has been conducted to determine the average radii of these clusters.  Based on HST observations, a new empirical formula has been developed to estimate the light profile of one-age star clusters using a single parameter - the half-mass radius.  By applying this formula to a set of realistic model clusters, a new method was established for retrieving genuine cluster radii from contaminated images.  A distinct correlation was discovered between the radii of young star clusters and the mass of their parent galaxies.  Clusters located within the central regions of galaxies exhibit enhanced radii when compared to mid-radius clusters, a phenomenon also observed in the Milky Way.  Various physical processes are responsible for this radial variation, including supernova explosions, gas dynamics, and phase mixing.  A theoretical model has been utilized to deconstruct the mid-radius cluster radius and the central enhanced cluster radius components, revealing that the former is composed of a supernova-driven expansion and a phase mixing contraction, while the latter is driven by gas dynamics.  A prediction has been made that the cluster radius of the Milky Way will be approximately 1.5 pc when observed with the Hubble Space Telescope in the near infrared.  A predicted cluster radius-shape ratio relationship exists at radii greater than 2 pc.  Two distinct types of globular clusters have been identified based on their light profiles, a finding that could be linked to the formation history of the Milky Way. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. For instance, our model resolves the sign problem in the Hubbard model on 36-site lattices at finite temperatures, making possible the concurrent Monte Carlo simulation of multiple fillings beyond half-filling. Moreover, we observe excellent agreement between our results and established theoretical and experimental data for quantities such as the double-spinon susceptibility and the spectral function at half-filling, both in the one-dimensional Hubbard model. Furthermore, our model finds solution for the electronic structure and the spectral weight of the two-dimensional Hubbard model at half-filling, showing agreement with existing data and providing insight into the movement of electrons as a function of the bandwidth. As a further demonstration of its effectiveness, our model determines the critical doping level for the onset of antiferromagnetic order in the Hubbard model. As antiferromagnetism is crucial to understanding superconductivity in cuprate materials, this finding paves the way for the model's application to studies of superconductivity. Our model's exceptional performance is attributed to its ability to accurately represent the interaction potential, achieving a significant reduction in the variance, thereby speeding up the convergence. With further optimization, this model has the potential to tackle even more complex many-body systems. Our open-source code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ComplexNeuralNetworks/ComplexNeuralNetworks.git. Additionally, we present a corresponding theoretical framework for the complex-valued affine coupling layer in the companion paper arXiv:2205.01206. Furthermore, we explore the application of this model to the study of rotational motion in molecular systems in the companion paper arXiv:2207.02629. Additionally, we present an analysis of the model's performance on the study of fermionic systems in the companion paper arXiv:2207.02630. Lastly, we present an discussion on the model's extension to nonlinear Hamiltonians in the companion paper arXiv:2207.02632.

This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we now derive a more general formula for counting y-friable integers up to x for $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern where the count of y-friable integers up to x for $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$ is approximately $\frac{x \rho_1((\log x)/\log y)}{\log x}$ and the count of y-friable integers up to x for $y \ll \log x$ is approximately $\frac{x \rho_1((\log x)/\log y)}{\log x} + \frac{x \rho_2((\log x)/\log y)}{(\log x)^2}$. 

In addition, we also provide a lower bound for $\rho_1(\lambda)$, which is currently the strongest lower bound for $\rho_1$ available. It states that for any nonnegative real number $\lambda \le 1$, the value of $\rho_1(\lambda)$ is greater than or equal to $1 - \frac{1+\lambda}{\sqrt{2}}$. 

We derived these results by first establishing a new upper bound for the counting function $S(x,y)$, which represents the number of y-friable integers up to x for $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. It is based on majorant functions including the Dirichlet L-functions and is achievable assuming the RH. Without making any assumptions, we obtained an alternative upper bound for $S(x,y)$. Both of these upper bounds led to further derivations including a new estimate for the frequency of y-friable integers up to x for $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$ and a new perspective on the distribution of y-friable integers up to x for $y \ll \log x$.

The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and grid search. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. These findings provide valuable insights into the performance of hyperparameter tuning algorithms in private deep learning. Interestingly, our experiments revealed that simple algorithms like evolutionary optimization and Bayesian methods often outperform the optimized optimizer algorithm for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. Additionally, our results demonstrate the efficacy of Bayesian optimization in tuning the hyperparameters of the private overOptimizer when the search space is large. This is an unexpected discovery, as the performance gains from such efficient hyperparameter tuning extend to non-optimal configurations, indicating that a balance between performance and privacy can be achieved with a smaller search space. These observations lead to a limitation of the current private overOptimizer, suggesting the need for a simple and efficient hyperparameter tuning method to maintain a balance between performance and privacy. Moreover, our experiments with a large search space lead to an interesting conclusion regarding the challenge of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, as achieving a balance between performance and privacy requires careful consideration of the cost of additional iterations. This is exemplified by the fact that the robust optimizer's performance is often inferior to that of the standard optimizer in private deep learning, highlighting the necessity to re-examine the design of private hyperparameter tuning algorithms through the lens of the high cost associated with additional iterations. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been developed and consistently applied, resulting in independent estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster at 19.9 megaparsecs with a 2.5 megaparsec margin of error. Additionally, a distinctive gap was discovered in the frequency distribution of galaxy distances, consistent with previous theoretical predictions made by Tomio. This study further contributes to the understanding of galaxy evolution within clusters by analyzing galaxy interactions based on their relative positions within the Fornax cluster, and identifying distinct population structures that influence each other's gravitational interactions. Furthermore, by analyzing large-scale structures within the Fornax cluster, a distinct line or "wall" has been identified at approximately 1800 kiloparsecs from the Earth on the celestial south side, extending from the galaxy NGC 1395, and has been given the codename "The Southern Wall". Additionally, a distinctive feature or "hole" has been identified within this structure, located at approximately 1300 megaparsecs from the Earth, and has been given the codename "The Antihubble Hole". A separate study has been conducted on the motion of galaxy pairs and small groups within the Fornax cluster, and has revealed a distinctive feature or "turnaround zone" located at approximately 800 kiloparsecs from the Earth on the celestial south side, and has been given the codename "The Southern Turnaround".

The primary objective of a classifier's training is to minimize its error rate on a given task. Yet, achieving this goal involves selecting a suitable loss function, which can significantly influence both the training process and the resulting model performance. This paper's initial section delims the myriad loss functions in use today. It then outlines a systematic method for evaluating loss function variations, focusing on two key aspects: 1) the impact of overfitting, which is addressed through regularization techniques; and 2) the effect of dataset characteristics, which is explored through both theoretical and practical considerations. This research is exemplified by a exploration of loss function variations for training ResNet50 on the CIFAR-10 dataset. The findings reveal that, when evaluating deep learning models, consideration should be given to both their general performance and their ability to generalize across different datasets. The paper's conclusions and future research directions are also discussed. Moreover, all experiments conducted as part of this study are reproducible, with the source code available online. This research is relevant to both practitioners and theoretical developers of loss functions. For the former, it provides a clear framework for creating and evaluating new loss function variations. For the latter, it offers both a clear framework and a method for testing its applicability to deep learning in classification contexts. This is achieved through a case study of one of the most widely used models and datasets. However, the proposed framework is applicable to other models and datasets as well. With the current explosion of deep learning applications across various domains and data sets, understanding its fundamental characteristics is more essential than ever. This research is a step forward in valuing simplicity and ease of interpretation as first-order properties of deep learning models. This is in line with the spirit of Charles Babbage's original vision of using computers to study computers. Finally, this research is also a demonstration of a successful scientific experiment on learning and understanding deep learning. The paper's conclusions are also supported by a new theoretical analysis of loss function variations, which is presented. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. By establishing a specific inequality, we demonstrate the existence of a global attractor for the controlled system. Key conditions for the controller's effectiveness are identified in terms of the skew-product structure. Furthermore, we prove that the control strategy achieves exponential stability for initial conditions near the equilibrium point. Additionally, we demonstrate the possibility of optimizing the controller to achieve optimal decay rates for specific boundary orientations. Our analysis is supported by numerical simulations, providing valuable insights into the dynamic behavior of the controlled system. 

For the two-dimensional case, we design a boundary feedback controller utilizing the wall shear stress, which suppresses vorticity modes and directs the flow towards its equilibrium state. Notably, this controller is compatible with turbulent flows having odd symmetry properties. Our study is an adaptation of the global feedback stabilization approach developed by Temam and Wang (2008) for the linear transport equation. 

In the three-dimensional setting, we design an oblique boundary feedback controller that suppresses specific eigenvector modes of the adjoint operator. By leveraging the inequality established in Section 3, we demonstrate the existence of a global attractor for the controlled system. Our study is an extension of the work by Liu and Zheng (2013) on the linear transport equation. 

The primary difference between the two-dimensional case studies lies in the orientation of the boundary feedback controller. In the two-dimensional case, the controller is oriented perpendicularly to the flow direction, whereas in the three-dimensional case, it is oriented obliquely.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining optimal expert demonstrations is a challenging and time-consuming task. Providing suboptimal actions can lead to the generation of costly and irrelevant feedback. We propose a new framework, called Online Corrective Feedback Learning (OCFL), which allows the agent to learn from any provided feedback, regardless of its form. We demonstrate that this framework subsumes previously established techniques, including PIL and reward learning, and showcases its effectiveness through the successful application of a simple OCFL meta-algorithm to a complex, real-world robotic task. Our results show that our approach yields superior performance when compared to existing methods. We also examine the challenges and limitations of our framework, as well as potential future directions, to which the answer is no. We believe that this framework holds great promise for any agent that can learn online, especially in settings where obtaining high-quality demonstrations is difficult or impractical. We hope that our work will inspire the development of new OCFL methods and the exploration of how our framework can be applied to other domains and applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a complex, real-world robotic task. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. In particular, our results indicate that in adverse channel conditions, CPM structures with higher rates can benefit from longer delay periods, whereas in more favorable conditions, lower rate CPMs are more effectively served. In addition, our work is applicable to any non-coherent differential CPM implementation. In practice, this could involve applying the derived delay optimization to the uplink transmission in wireless communication systems. Our theoretical findings and associated computer simulations both support the delay optimization strategy, offering a useful strategy for designing and evaluating the performance of non-coherent CPM modems. In conclusion, delayed conventional differential detection performance can be optimized through increased delay periods, achieving a notable error rate reduction in comparison to untreated differential detection. In particular, our results indicate a 6 dB SNR gain at a 10% error rate for the (128,64,4) CPM modulation, demonstrating the effectiveness of this strategy in enhancing the robust performance of wireless communication systems. In addition, our work has also verified that in some scenarios, the application of delay periods can result in a greater than 10 dB SNR gain at the same error rate for certain CPM formats, such as (64,32,4) and (32,16,4) in both time-dispersion and frequency-dispersion channels.
