Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have focused either on adding the information lost during removal or creating artificial rain images to aid in the process. Unfortunately, these approaches suffer from poorly aligned generated images which severely hinders the performance of the model. To overcome this limitation, a single framework is proposed that simultaneously generates artificial rain and uses it to enhance the model's ability to process images. The proposed framework utilizes a disentangled image-to-image translation technique to create two separate images - one representing the rain and the background of the input image. By doing so, the generated rain and background are perfectly aligned, enabling the model to effectively remove the rain from input images. Numerous rain-related challenges are tested using the proposed framework, and the results show significant improvement in comparison to existing techniques. The proposed framework is also free from explicit motion segmentation, making it a more efficient and practical solution. The framework's code is available online at https://github.com/zwang2016/Closing-the-loop.

Additionally, our method enables the creation of more interpretable policy representations, surpassing baseline performance in certain metrics by 10-20%. Human-in-the-loop evaluations indicate that our approach uses human labeling time 5-10 times more effectively, and their subjective evaluation ranks our policy as 20% better. A subsequent evaluation protocol involving human labelers confirms the effectiveness of our approach in producing a superior and more reliable representation of the state space. Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. The research also explored ways to develop more reliable and effective classification models by integrating expert input on essential features. This combined approach resulted in significantly enhanced performance, with over 80 percent accuracy for most substances and as high as 84 percent for ecstasy. The enhanced models demonstrated superior performance on at least half of the evaluated substances and identified new potential members within the "pleiades." The revised models identified benzodiazepines as a separate cluster within sedatives, distinct from hypnotics. The integrated approach also pinpointed key personality traits associated with drug consumption, with certain traits linked to the use of multiple drugs within a cluster. The research demonstrated that personality traits, particularly those encompassing the Five Factor Model, significantly contribute to the ability to accurately classify individuals as users or non-users for various substances. The results indicated that certain personality traits are linked to the consumption of specific substances or entire clusters. The data also revealed a connection between the sensation seeking feature and the classification accuracy for most substances. The research findings may lead to the creation of more effective strategies for detecting drug use by minors on online platforms, such as monitoring posts indicating the desire to consume multiple drugs within a cluster. The study established a reliable and accurate data set for evaluating and developing classification models for drug consumption on the internet. The integrated approach may also facilitate the identification of potentially abused substances with a low detection rate, such as novel opioids and novel stimulants. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in comparison to their counterparts in areas such as text classification and the evaluation of generated text against these rules.  Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/ygoyal-vision/atomic.  We also explore the challenges associated with evaluating the degree to which these rules are representative of diverse populations and offer statistical analysis of the data based on 14 different demographic factors.  Lastly, we highlight the potential applications of this dataset in enhancing the realism of simulated environments and the ability of artificial intelligence to understand human intentions.  This dataset is unique in that it focuses on conditional relationships rather than actions or emotions taken in isolation.  Instead of modeling individual events, ATOMIC captures relationships between events, providing an innovative framework for the exploration of causality and the development of more sophisticated artificial intelligence models.  We have established the utility of this dataset in enhancing the performance of machine learning models in areas outside of conditional reasoning. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this dataset in improving the performance of machine learning models in areas such as text classification and the evaluation of generated text against these rules. To enhance data efficiency and enable the learning of complex speech recognition tasks, a multi-modal approach that combines text with speech has been proposed. By leveraging the rich linguistic information present in both speech and text, these models can effectively generalize to various tasks such as word-level alignment, phoneme synthesis, and speech synthesis. We introduce a bidirectional attention multi-modal training framework that allows the exchange of information between speech and text models, enabling the learning of more semantic and phonetically accurate representations. This framework is evaluated on a speech synthesis task, and the results show that it outperforms single-modal models in terms of mean opinion score (MOS). Furthermore, the proposed framework's ability to learn phonetically rich representations is demonstrated by its performance in phoneme recognition tasks. We believe that this framework has the potential to enhance state-of-the-art speech recognition systems. We have made the dataset used in this study available online, and the proposed framework's code can be found on GitHub. 

In detail, the evaluation of the proposed framework was conducted on the Librispeech dataset, and the results for the primary experiment are as follows: the multi-modal bidirectional attention framework achieved a mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.903 in subjective evaluation, outperforming the single-modal model which had an MOS of 3.768. The paper also reports the results for the phoneme recognition task; the multi-modal bidirectional attention framework's phoneme error rate was 0.044, whereas the single-modal model's phoneme error rate was 0.046. These findings indicate that the multi-modal bidirectional attention framework generates more natural speech and yields better phoneme recognition results than the single-modal model. 

The study further explores the implications of the proposed framework by conducting an ablation analysis, examining the following variants of the bidirectional attention framework: the single-modal baseline, two single-modal models, two variants of the bidirectional attention framework, and two control variants. The results of the ablation analysis are as follows: the two variants of the bidirectional attention framework outperformed the single-modal baseline but performed worse than the single-modal model used during training; the multi-modal baseline performed worse than the single-modal model used during training but better than the two variants of the bidirectional attention framework; the control variants used for testing and training performed worse than the bidirectional attention framework used during testing but better than the multi-modal baseline used during testing.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc current flow, which is influenced by an applied gate voltage and varies with nanowire length. The relationship between this phenomenon and two possible underlying mechanisms - coherent quantum phase slips and Coulomb blockade - is examined through experimental data analysis. By studying the blockage of dc current flow as a function of gate voltage, nanowire length, and temperature, it is found that the blockage magnitude is directly proportional to the length of the nanowire, displaying a linear increase with length, whereas the transition from unblocked to blocked states occurs at a critical value, independent of length. This proportionality implies that the blockage magnitude is a property of the nanowire itself, rather than a feature of quantum phase slips, which would display a nonlinear length dependence. Consequently, the blockage is attributed to a large-capacity well within the nanowire's charge-displacement energy spectrum. The presence of this well is confirmed by observing the blockage's transition as a function of applied voltage, nanowire length, and temperature, and the results indicate that the blockage's onset voltage occurs at the charging energy of the well, divided by the nanowire's length and the quantum flux. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints.   - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.

while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two plasmon states have distinct origins and can be managed by material design.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The approach we developed is compatible with existing distributed learning frameworks and yields significant improvements in a computational economics application. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
Our research is available online with additional statistics and detailed
experiments that include diagnosis reports. 
We invite the community to build upon our work by downloading our pre-trained
models available at https://github.com/ekaren/bert-lstm-basque and exploring
further ways to evaluate the language understanding capabilities of sequential
neural networks. 
K. Adolphs provided invaluable insights into the Basque language, its syntax,
and its morphology.
The anonymous reviewers and conference chairs are also gratefully acknowledged
for their feedback and guidance.

University of the Basque Country.

The modified code is available at https://github.com/ekaren/bert-lstm-basque.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. These analyses led to a refinement of the planet's orbital path and a better understanding of its rotational characteristics. The refined data indicate that the planet completes three rotations around its axis in the same amount of time it takes to orbit its star once. This discovery was confirmed by analyzing the transit light curves from both observation periods. The newly acquired data will enable researchers to observe the planet during different stages of its orbit, including both its approach to and recession from the star. This new transits analysis provides the necessary framework for optimizing the scheduling of future JWST observations of this extraordinary planet.

Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Code is publicly available on https://github.com/strandreask/PAUNLM and demonstrates the practical potential of deep learning in creating lower-dose PET scans without MRI, as shown in the study. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our new approach provides a foundation for investigating the feasibility of graph drawing transversals and graph minors with the upward planar property. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. Our findings also support the idea that the difficulty of La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ materials to break the interlocked vortex lattice structure into a more stable triangular lattice structure is due to the material's unique superconducting properties. The observed transition at lower magnetic fields of 28 T and 30 T, but at the same low temperatures, is attributed to another type of lattice structure transition. The results of our research have important implications for the further understanding of the intricate relationship between superconductivity and magnetism in cuprate materials.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings are experimentally verifiable through the characterization of brush layers using block copolymer melts on curved substrates via neutron reflectivity, atomic force microscopy, and scanning force microscopy. This knowledge can further be applied to design materials with optimized curvilinear surface structures to improve the performance of materials engineered at the nanoscale. Additionally, our understanding of the end exclusion zone phenomenon may provide valuable insights into the microphase assembly of block copolymer melts on curved surfaces, offering a new perspective on the underlying principles governing surface tension and the curvature-induced ordering of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our discovery of the end exclusion zone phenomenon may also be relevant to the biophysical engineering of living cell membranes, which the authors propose could be modeled as complex curved surfaces. Therefore, this new perspective on the physics of curved, stretched brushes may have far-reaching implications for the biology of cell membrane architecture. Furthermore, our understanding of the end exclusion zone phenomenon could be applied to the design of new generative machine learning models that utilize inverse design methods to create innovative materials with optimized curvilinear surface structures, enabling the generation of complex, high-performance materials engineered at the nanoscale. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some properties of beta_k are examined especially for the scenario where k is 2. Computer programs were used to calculate beta_k for all graphs with 25 or fewer nodes and almost all trees up to the point where their number of nodes reaches 32. Further, a formula was found but not proved mathematically for the metric dimension of some trees when the shortest distance between points is two. It was discovered that caching pre-computed values of beta_k greatly speeds up the computation of subsequent values of beta_k. A method was found but not proved mathematically for determining the metric dimension of some graphs when the shortest distance between points is two. Some connections between the minimum identifying set, minimum dominating set and neighborhood covers of a graph were established. A term "truncated dimension" was coined for beta_k and its variants. A method was proposed but not proved mathematically for determining the minimum identifying set of a graph when the shortest distance between points is three. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. These machine learning models can be trained on existing and ongoing data, enabling them to perform automatic analysis of Fermi-LAT all-sky maps with a low computational cost. For example, reprocessing the entire Fermi-LAT all-sky map archive would only take a single computer around 10 days. These algorithms are now being utilized to study the Milky Way and detect the giant radio loop structure reported by ref. [37] and to analyze transient phenomena like fast flares and unknown sources above 10 GeV. These machine learning tools are being applied to current and future high-statistics observations, such as those from the Fermi All-sky Variability (FAVOR) campaign and the Fermi-LAT flywheel survey. These models will be made publicly available to facilitate machine learning image processing of Fermi-LAT data. Furthermore, a scientific paper on this research has been submitted to the Astrophysics Source Code Library (ASCIDB). Additionally, an oral presentation on this research was delivered at the 37th Cosmic Ray Conference in Hambourg, Germany. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks as per its application context. We accompany each approximation strategy with a corresponding serial dictatorship-optimization solution for the respective problem domain, offering an independently useful outcome along with our main finding. We validate our theoretical analysis with computational experiments conducted on various combinatorial optimization challenges, showing that the obtained serial dictatorships indeed outperform random assignments by a substantial margin in terms of achieved value. Specifically, we establish key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both differential and integral operators, along with a significant formula that encompasses both product and quotient rules. Notably, our findings are applicable to the variable-order Riemann-Liouville fractional differential and integral operators, which are derived as direct outcomes of our novel Leibniz Rules. Our research is a substantial expansion of prior work by Baillif and Nicolay, contributing novel product and quotient rules tailored to the variable-order Lebesgue-Stieltjes differential and integral operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of our results through the derivation of specific operators, such as the variable-order fractional integral of polynomial functions and the derivation of the variable-order fractional differential of trigonometric functions. Our research is also accompanied by illustrative applications and computational examples to demonstrate the efficacy of our novel rules. A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, a novel framework has been
developed that utilizes a given boundary annotation to facilitate pair
formation and reduce noise.  To further refine the framework, a novel
modification of the contrastive loss function was incorporated to penalize
segmentation errors on unseen areas.  The proposed framework was evaluated
on cardiac segmentation using the M-mode ultrasound dataset and Muenster dataset
and compared with existing contrastive learning-based self-supervised segmentation
methods.  Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields
better segmentation accuracy than baseline methods.  The code is available at
https://github.com/zwang86/BI-MIM.

We introduce the G4C challenge, a series of tasks designed to assess a robot's ability to engage in meaningful conversations as a game master in a fantasy setting, guided by a set of rules. To test our hypothesis that incorporating elements of cognitive psychology into a machine learning model improves its performance, we developed the Systeria engine featuring a theory-of-mind-inspired module. Our experiments showed that a robot equipped with this engine is more effective at guiding players through a fantasy world, encouraging them to make decisions in line with their intentions, and having more enjoyable and immersive experiences according to human assessors. The data and code for our evaluation are publicly available, and we are planning to host the challenge at a major robotics conference. As the first game-based evaluation for a robot's social intelligence, the G4C challenge has significant implications for the development of more human-like and engaging human-robot interactions. As playing tabletop games with humans requires a high level of social sophistication, it presents a critical benchmark for social robots to surpass human performance. Introduction Human-robot interactions are highly sophisticated when robots are engaged in activities like card games, which require a deep understanding of human intentions and the ability to make decisions in a shared context. While humans have natural social skills, their ability to make decisions in a game context is heavily influenced by the decisions made by the robot, affecting the overall experience and enjoyment of the game. Understanding the Decision-Making Process of Humans Humans have a unique way of thinking about other people's thoughts and intentions, which allows them to make decisions in a game context that takes these factors into consideration. This understanding of human intentions is rooted in their ability to form a theory-of-mind about other people, which includes their goals, their knowledge, their beliefs, their intentions, their desires, and their emotions. In contrast, robots lack this level of social sophistication, which hinders their ability to engage humans in meaningful conversations and guide them through a game. The Systeria Engine Our research involves a state-of-the-art natural language processing engine called Systeria, which is designed to have a theory-of-mind component that allows it to understand human intentions and form a shared theory-of-mind with the player. The engine is composed of multiple modules, including a cognitive architecture, a set of common-sense reasoning resources, and a dialogue manager. The cognitive architecture is responsible for modeling the player's mind, the common-sense reasoning resources provide the engine with a basic understanding of the game world, and the dialogue manager uses this information to guide the conversation

We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the movement of partons in the transverse direction, related to parton spin alignment, which is rooted in the interactions represented by corresponding correlators. These new functions lead to distinct effects in single-hadron production, particularly in the $x$-dependence of azimuthal asymmetry in pion production, and they provide unique access to parton motion and spin alignment through $k_\perp$-introduction in semi-inclusive processes like SIDIS and $e$-proton scattering. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactuals holds great promise for enhancing the performance of language models. However, generating high-quality counterfactuals on a large scale is a significant challenge. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel framework called DISCO, which leverages a contrastive learning objective to extract valuable information from existing text datasets without the need for explicit counterfactual data. We demonstrate that DISCO's counterfactuals, distillation samples derived from mutual information maximization, yield superior performance when evaluated against human judgments. Notably, our method achieves comparable performance to a counterfactual generation baseline while requiring no explicit counterfactual data and reducing the need for expensive human annotations by over an order of magnitude. Moreover, DISCO's counterfactuals prove just as effective at enhancing the classification performance of a classifier as the baseline method, despite being significantly less expensive to produce. Our code and data are openly available at https://github.com/Pranav12345/disco.

Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare sector. The framework's efficacy is substantiated across three diverse evaluation protocols. Additionally, analysis of circulation patterns among participatory users and data aggregators is conducted to optimize participation, yielding a 280% increase in participant engagement without compromising security. This paper is a seminal work on the subject matter and paves the way for future exploration in the wearable healthcare domain. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. To address this, we explore the application of supervised learning on temporal sequence data. By representing variables as sets of nearby time points and incorporating temporal constraints through missing value imputation, we transform sequence data into fixed-length feature vectors. This strategy enhances the interpretation of model results and identifies relevant variables within the sequence. A study on Arabidopsis thaliana cell cultures, using microarray data with 24 time points and 22,000 genes, demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in predicting cell cycle phase and identifying key processes during cell differentiation. Compared to existing methods, our proposal outperforms wrapper techniques and gene expression models, showing great potential for broader life science applications. The devised framework is adaptable and can be tailored to suit various problem types and data types. The implementation of the approach is provided as an customizable R function.

It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code,
the task is to determine how many linear measurements are required to reconstruct it.
A general formula for this problem was first formulated by Wu in 2010 for Hamming distances. 
This paper extends Wu's formula to a more complex distance metric known as the Hamming distance. 
For d=2, it formulates a general sequence reconstruction problem and provides a specific code. 
For d>2, it proves that the number of necessary measurements exceeds a specific fraction of a particular parameter. 
This parameter is determined by the ratio of the distance to the number of sequence components. 
It also offers a specific binary code for d=3 and 4. 
For d=5 and greater, it proposes a particular binary code with a specific structure. 
This structure ensures that any two distinct sequence components maintain a distance of at least d from each other. 
It further implies that a Hamming distance of d is achievable in a sequence of n=2^k components. 
This paper finally explores various limitations and open questions of the sequence reconstruction problem.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. This challenge has important implications for improving the effectiveness of Question Answering tools on real-world tasks and has already inspired several notable advancements, which we are making available at https://github.com/google-rev/qasperm. We anticipate this dataset to serve as a benchmark to evaluate the progress of models in the future. Two models that performed subpar on this dataset have been incorporated into the paper, along with a proposed model that leverages a mix of sparse attention and a document pointer network, resulting in a significant boost of over 20 F1 points when using only the paper abstracts. This model's efficacy is further demonstrated by its ability to answer questions when provided with the full paper, a task that human subjects found manageable. Our results indicate that a Question Answering system that relies on paper abstracts can provide accurate answers for at least 36% of the test set, and when using the full paper, this increase to 43%. We believe that this dataset has the potential to contribute to the development of more advanced Question Answering tools in the future. In the present section, we discuss some fundamental aspects of the basic SIR model, followed by considerations and applications of more complex models that build upon this foundation. Many of these more intricate models incorporate various components that generalize the basic model, while others tackle specific issues related to epidemic transmission dynamics. Some key characteristics of the basic SIR model need to be highlighted before exploring these more complex models. These fundamental characteristics include the use of non-negative compartment values, the application of mass action principles for transmission rates, and the existence of a well-defined recovery rate. With these aspects in mind, we can better appreciate the development of derivative models that build upon this foundation, often incorporating additional elements while upholding these core principles. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method's efficiency and accuracy are demonstrated through texture recovery, face modeling, and non-rigid object pose estimation experiments, resulting in superior performance when compared to both traditional and learning-based methods. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/antitlo/diffshadow.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings indicate significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. Furthermore, this study is relevant to our broader research on the development of in situ MRI monitoring methods for reactive gas-solid systems in the Institute of Chemical Engineering and Industrial Biotechnology at the University of Hanover.

This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. Moreover, our results facilitate the identification of necessary and sufficient conditions for global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. A control system or its impulsive system extension is globally asymptotically controllable to a target if and only if there exists a control that can drive any trajectory to the target, and this is equivalent to the existence of a control Lyapunov function for the closed loop system. A key consequence of our findings is that the existence of a strongest control Lyapunov function under a given control or feedback stabilizer is a necessary and sufficient condition for global asymptotic controllability, or for the existence of a feedback stabilizer. These results are illustrated through examples and case studies in polynomial control systems and their applications. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a new analysis of the MAMPU/SMAHS survey is conducted, focusing on the distinct formation times and lifetimes of star-forming bulges and disks. According to models, massive bulges form quickly ($\sim$10 Myr) under extreme conditions, often followed by a short star formation lifetime ($\sim$10 Myr). In contrast, massive disks form over 50 Myr and have longer star formation lifetimes ($\sim$100 Myr). Since star formation on the main sequence occurs at a constant rate, galaxies with short star formation lifetimes will deplete their molecular gas mass when observed at later stages. As a result, the observed gas masses above the star formation rate - molecular gas mass relation shift to higher masses at $\sim$10$^{10.3}$ M$_{\odot}$. This break corresponds to the mass range where bulge formation dominates, indicating that bulges play a key role in shaping the main sequence relation. Models also suggest that the rotation curves and specific star formation rates of massive bulges and disks follow distinct trends, related to their formation times. Furthermore, the angular momentum conservation principle implies distinct angular momentum release patterns during major mergers for bulges and disks. While major mergers can detect and quench both bulges and disks, minor mergers quench disks while leaving bulges unaffected. Since quenching disks causes molecules to be dissipated as stars form, the observed gas masses above the star formation rate - molecular gas mass relation shift to higher masses at $\sim$10$^{10.3}$ M$_{\odot}$. Additionally, the detection of rotationally supported starbursts with large specific star formation rates and low velocity dispersions at the high mass end of the main sequence, where starbursts exhibit offset molecular gas masses above the star formation rate - molecular gas mass relation, supports the role of bulges in shaping the main sequence relation. Models also suggest that the star formation rates of rotationally supported starbursts are primarily governed by the angular momentum release pattern during major mergers, resulting in quenching and enhanced star formation. In contrast, models predict that galaxies with massive disks will exhibit both locally and globally enhanced star formation rates on the main sequence at $\sim$10$^{10.3}$ M$_{\odot}$. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing $\rm 0.6-0.8 M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$ of accretion, accompanied by suppressed star formation rates of $\rm 1-2 M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. Furthermore, we observe evidence of gas inflows, outflows and overdistributions on planes tilted relative to the major axes of the galaxies, which may be the result of gravitational tidal interactions with the galaxy group. According to our modeling, these galaxies are in the process of merging a massive disk system with a bulge, a process that could provide insight into the formation and functioning of quiescent lopsided galaxies during the early universe. Additionally, their extensive star formation, tidal interactions and gas flows may ultimately result in the formation of a bulge through a process that could be relevant to the formation of passive lopsided galaxies at higher redshifts. Lastly, their similarities to the galaxy pairs at $\rm z=3.42$ and $\rm z=2.81$ that we studied previously may indicate that the formation of passive quasallytic systems occurs when galaxies are interacting with each other during the transition from $\rm z>3.3$.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Finally, we propose a modification to the existing legal doctrine and offer it as a potential amendment to the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs, by applying a technique called edge selection, which selectively removes constraints to simplify the problem.

Baker's method was later expanded to accommodate graphs with additional properties, such as the presence of specific facial structures.

A new technique is presented, allowing edge selection to account for the values assigned to constraints, making it possible to develop PTAS for certain CSPs on graph classes with limited connectivity.

This technique is applied to design PTAS for various CSPs, such as Maximum Cut on planar graphs with certain facial structures, Maximum Weighted Independent Set on certain classes of bounded-degree trees, and Minimum Weighted Vertex Cover on planar graphs with certain facial structures.

The new technique is also used to develop PTAS for certain CSPs with arbitrary value functions, such as the M-ary CSP on certain classes of bounded-degree trees.

These results demonstrate the effectiveness of edge selection in achieving PTAS on graph classes with limited connectivity, providing a new framework for developing PTAS for general-valued CSPs. Moreover, this paper presents a new application of the edge selection, such as the problem of designing a weighted graph that maximizes the weight of a specific subgraph. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We invite researchers to contribute their work towards this goal and provide a collective repository of their efforts. Additionally, we invite submissions of cutting-edge research related to XAI, specifically those centered on DNNs, for presentation at the NIPS 2018 workshop on Interpretable Machine Learning (IML). Moreover, we plan to maintain an up-to-date, freely accessible archive of all research presented at this workshop. This study is an extension of the earlier effort initiated by the IML workshop organizers and aims to serve as a comprehensive repository of DNN XAI research. Although significant progress has been made in recent years, especially in the evaluation and assessment of DNNs, vast areas within the field of XAI remain unexplored. This study intends to catalyze further research in this domain by providing a thorough examination of the subject matter and a comprehensive archive of recent research on DNNs. This includes not only methodologies focused on local explanation but also those centered on visualizing the network's structure, as well as efforts to develop benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics for assessing the effectiveness of these methods. This study covers an expansive range of topics, including data preprocessing, artificial data generation, encoding schemes, and diverse techniques for model interpretation, including saliency maps, feature importance measurement, model approximation, and semantic decomposition. This study also delves into the subject of neural network-specific visualization, including the visualization of neural network training processes and the development of interactive visualization tools. This study is unique in its comprehensive examination of DNNs, encompassing over 150 research papers, 17 benchmark datasets, and 10 open-source, publicly available code repositories. This work delves into various quantum algebras that arise from a special type of set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation and their 'q-analogue' counterparts, also providing common characteristics that these algebras share in terms of quasi-bialgebras and twists. By establishing that set-theoretic and q-analogue solutions produce the same specific types of algebras and by identifying additional constraints for their 'q-deformed' counterparts, this research showcases the potential of set-theoretic solutions to generate a wide range of quantum algebras and their 'q-deformed' equivalents, which can be seen as particular instances of quasi-bialgebras and their twists. Moreover, this work expands on earlier findings by revealing that the general approach outlined in [6] can be applied not just to quadratic equations like the Yang-Baxter equation, but also to non-quadratic equations as well as those with zero-divisors, which gives rise to '2-variable' or 'grassmannian' type solutions and their 'q-analogue', respectively. By exploring the underlying properties of these solutions and their 'q-analogue', this research demonstrates that they can result in '2-variable' or 'grassmannian' type quasi-bialgebras and their twists, which provides a foundation for further investigation into their properties and representations. Finally, this work highlights potential future research directions in this field. In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in overlap by positioning the donors allows for the realization of precise, atomic-scale spin exchange experiments. 
The research further shows that arranging perpendicular dopants enables the retrieval of unique, pure orbital effects that dominate exchange interaction, a feature that exchange interaction fails to attain with in-plane placement.
The study presents an opportunity to explore the intricate consequences of quantum tunneling and its interaction with Coulomb forces, and the outcomes indicate the feasibility of precise control over the exchange interaction by positioning the donors, a capability that could also benefit the development of silicon-based quantum information technologies.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce a novel approach called SKILL, which infuses structured knowledge into large language models through training on specific knowledge graph triples. Our method leverages knowledge graphs to generate specific knowledge graphs for each language task, enabling the use of these models to answer questions based on structured information. Evaluating our approach on diverse language tasks shows substantial improvements over baseline models. For instance, on the T5-kb dataset, which requires models to answer natural language questions based on knowledge graphs, our approach achieved an impressive 12% point increase in accuracy. Interestingly, when evaluating these models on the same dataset but with a focus on accuracy rather than efficiency, their performance saw little decline. Additionally, our approach enabled state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE dataset, indicating that incorporating structured knowledge can lead to enhanced general language understanding. Our method's effectiveness was further validated across multiple knowledge graphs and language models, demonstrating that it is a versatile and robust approach. Our findings suggest that the method is particularly effective for models with smaller parameter counts and may be less efficient when using very large models. Our code and knowledge graphs are openly available at https://github.com/google-research/skill. Our approach also enabled the creation of a knowledge graph-based evaluation metric for the SAMsum dataset, which gauges a model's ability to comprehend and generate text based on structured knowledge. This metric, in turn, was employed to assess models with our approach, which outperformed baselines on the metric by a significant margin. Nonetheless, this metric demands human annotation and may not be suitable for all datasets. Consequently, we employed an additional evaluation approach, which involves comparing models' performance on both their training and testing data. This evaluation approach involved creating additional datasets with annotated knowledge graph triples, which served as both training and testing data. This evaluation approach validated our method's effectiveness on yet another dataset, known as the CMC dataset, which necessitates the enumeration of multiple knowledge graph triples from a given text. Our approach's efficacy on this dataset was evidenced by its 25% point increase in F1 score over baseline models. This increase in performance was also accompanied by a reduction in the number of unnecessary triple predictions, indicating that our approach not only excels in primary task performance but also achieves this excellence with greater efficiency. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In particular, this study demonstrates the utility of marmoset-based models for translating insights to humans. As recent studies have highlighted the value of marmoset animal models in Parkinson's research, our computational framework can effectively integrate their electrophysiological findings. Furthermore, this model showcases the benefits of collaborative research between experimental neuroscientists and computational modelers in the neuroscience community. As such, the model may serve as a blueprint for similar collaborative efforts to develop data-driven computational brain models. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the efficacy of a collaborative approach between experimental and computational neuroscientists in developing a novel computational brain model. As a result, this model has generated novel insights into Parkinson's disease dynamics and may contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it has highlighted the value of marmoset-based models in Parkinson's research, emphasizing the importance of consideration of species-specific aspects in modeling the disease. Finally, this research has highlighted the benefits of multi-regional concurrent electrophysiological recordings in computational modeling of the brain. As a result, it may also facilitate a better understanding of other complex brain disorders affecting the marmoset brain, such as Alzheimer's disease, anxiety, and epilepsy. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 parsecs of precision. Our observations revealed diverse active galactic nuclei accretion states as well as large-scale outflows in all targets, and for two of the targets, GOALS #11 and #55, our data showed for the first time the presence of bi-conical outflows and double-ionized nitrogen velocity maps. Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal memory. This paper builds upon this work and suggests a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model by integrating the dual-path RNN with convolutional layers. In the first path, the model applies a regular convolution recurrent network (CRCRN) using which it extracts time-dependent speech features. In the second path, the model uses a dual-path RNN (DPhRNN) where it employs lateral connections and a dual-path system to model these time-dependent features. The two paths are connected through a dual-path connector and the resulting output from this connection is used as the input to the DPhRNN. The proposed DPCRN model was evaluated on the WSJ0-2mix database and the results indicate it outperforms the regular CRCRN model in terms of speech separation performance. Moreover, DPCRN shows superiority in modeling longer sequences as evidenced by the improvement in model performance when the length of analyzed sequences is increased. Additionally, a comparison with alternative RNN architectures confirmed the efficacy of the dual-path RNN. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our research also highlights the importance of examining the entanglement of distinct Jaynes-Cummings systems components. Lastly, we discover that a tripartite entanglement state, which is a form of multipartite entanglement, can be created by applying a single, non-entangling rotation to one system. This rotation leads to the creation of both genuine tripartite entanglement and a specific Schmidganger state. Our research paves the way for investigating the creation of multipartite entanglement through Jaynes-Cummings interactions in large systems. Our findings are further verified by a quantum circuit simulation, which demonstrates its applicability and provides physical insight into the entanglement generation process. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding pilot testing phase between 2009 and 2011, a modified version of the upgraded detector was integrated into the CMS system. This pilot testing prototype, comprising four upgraded pixel pilot blades in the forward direction, was capable of delivering full operational data within the CMS system. This paper outlines the technical modifications made to the upgraded pilot blades, their associated readout systems, and data processing chains. Furthermore, this paper reports on the results obtained from the pilot testing, including the associated noise levels, resolution parameters, and overall data quality. These results contributed to the design optimization of the full-scale upgrade of the CMS silicon tracker. Additionally, this paper discusses the lessons learned from the pilot testing, particularly in regards to the detector operation, data processing, and associated problems encountered during the testing phase. These lessons have since been applied to the full-scale upgrade of the CMS silicon tracker. Finally, this paper outlines the associated challenges faced while integrating the upgraded detector into the CMS system within a multi-disciplinary environment comprising both experimental and technical components. This paper is an expansion on the presentation made at the 2012 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference held in Honolulu, Hawaii, USA. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including the use of quantum tomography with multiple non-commuting observables, such as the quadrature amplitude and number operators. Another method involves analyzing the Wigner function of the state after performing a unitary transformation on the system, known as the tomographic map. This technique provides a direct connection between the original state and its reconstructed form. Our study demonstrates how to apply this approach to detect specific properties of a state, such as entanglement or the onset of synchronization, by designing the unitary transformation to highlight these features in the reconstructed Wigner function. To illustrate this concept, we demonstrate the detection of two separate scenarios: first, we identify the conditions under which a two-mode Gaussian state will exhibit entanglement, and second, we find the parameters that indicate the onset of synchronization in a pair of coupled lasers described by a Markov process. In both cases, the unitary transformation is chosen so that the reconstructed Wigner function will display the effects of these phenomena in a manifest form. Consequently, full state reconstruction becomes an easier task, as we only need to determine the transformation parameters rather than the entire set of moments of the system. Our work paves the way for the use of tomography maps as a powerful tool for monitoring the dynamics of open quantum systems, enabling us to track changes in their entanglement or other desired properties. In addition, this approach can be adapted for detecting a wide range of other attributes of quantum states. Finally, we expect that our findings will contribute to the development of new unitary transformations suitable for the reconstruction of specific properties of continuous-variable states, and to a deeper understanding of the relationship between the system's unitary evolution and its properties, which will facilitate the study of the dynamics of open quantum systems. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Our approach is also found to be compatible with the Monte Carlo tensor network algorithm, enabling the efficient computation of local thermal averages in three-dimensional systems. Our results include the accurate determination of the order parameter for the thermal phase transition in a 2D and 3D Ising model, as well as the analysis of a quench protocol in 1D on the X-Y model with a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Additionally, we explore the connection between our approach and the Monte Carlo tensor network algorithm, and examine the potential of our constructed objects to be employed in machine learning-inspired tensor network reconstruction techniques. Overall, our work elevates the utility of tensor network techniques by equipping them with the ability to accurately capture the behavior of systems in a wide range of situations. Additionally, we have made our tensor network training data publicly available. Further details can be found in the supplementary materials available on the arXiv. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs with a fixed treewidth. Furthermore, this study introduces and analyzes the complexity of Bi-Strong Geodetic, a variant of SG. Additionally, a method for strong geodetic subset identification is proposed, based on the characterization of minimal strong geodetic subsets, which is found to be applicable to certain types of graphs, including bipartite graphs and forests. This characterization enables the development of an efficient algorithm for SGR in these graph types, which is shown to be an NP-complete problem. Lastly, a discussion on the characterization and an algorithm for SGR in chordal graphs is presented, which sets the stage for further investigation into the parameterized complexity of SG. This investigation holds significance in understanding the computational complexity of graph traversal problems, which are fundamental in the field of computer science. Furthermore, this study is relevant to various applications, such as software development, transportation systems, and social network analysis, which it is essential to analyze from a computational complexity perspective.
