The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still convey information about the task's dynamics, specifically about what paths to avoid. We introduce TRAIL, a new imitation learning framework that leverages this insight by learning a value function that represents the optimal return of a task, and uses it to prioritize the most useful expert examples. Unlike previous methods that rely on assuming the expert examples are drawn randomly from a fixed distribution, TRAIL makes no such assumptions. Instead, it assumes the expert examples are drawn from a unknown distribution that isn't necessarily representative of the overall distribution of suboptimal paths. We prove that by making a few assumptions about this distribution and the data, we can obtain a policy that is nearly as good as the one obtained using all the expert examples, with a high probability. We evaluate TRAIL on a variety of tasks, including navigation tasks in complex environments and a simulation of a difficult robotic insertion task, and find that it significantly outperforms other imitation learning methods that assume the expert examples are random. TRAIL's success suggests that it can efficiently use a large amount of low-quality data to obtain a good policy, which could be very useful in a variety of applications. We also show that suboptimal data that seems irrelevant at first glance can still be very useful for imitation, and that the amount of time it takes for TRAIL to obtain a good policy can vary greatly, depending on a variety of factors. We hope to use these insights to further improve imitation learning algorithms in the future. We compare TRAIL to several other imitation learning algorithms that assume the expert examples are drawn randomly from a fixed distribution, including maximum likelihood estimation, robust imitation learning, and a new method called efficient imitation learning. We find that these methods obtain policies that are significantly worse than TRAIL's, with a high probability. We also compare the performance of TRAIL on a variety of tasks, and find that it outperforms these methods on all of them. We release the code and data that we used to evaluate TRAIL, and hope that it will be useful to other researchers. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Notably, we observe our approach to achieve comparable performance to supervisor-assisted reinforcement learning and outperforms independent reinforcement learning training in complex tasks requiring both exploration and efficient exploitation of peer agent experiences. The proposed framework also exhibits adaptable performance in scenarios with an excessive number of peer agents and a striking resistance to hyperparameter changes, exhibiting a notable increase in data efficiency over traditional reinforcement learning methods in complex domains requiring both exploration and efficient exploitation of peer agent experiences. Key implementations of our framework are also highlighted in an accompanying video available at https://youtu.be/6Q6CQ8KfHgA. The proposed framework's potential applications are particularly suitable for peer-agent collaborations in multi-agent scenarios and our research lays the groundwork for further development of our approach. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Moreover, our method demonstrates effective performance in challenging scenarios such as varying lighting conditions and cluttered backgrounds, enabling reliable and repetitive pose estimation and end-effector positioning in real-world environments. The system's simplicity and the absence of fiducial markers make it suitable for dynamic scenes and applications where the robot and camera are mounted on moving bases. The method's applicability is demonstrated through successful execution of complex robotic tasks in real-world scenarios. The system's code is available for public access. The method's limitations suggest further potential for enhancing robustness and achieving sub-millimeter precision. The system's performance could be optimized with a more efficient machine learning model, while the application for dynamic scenes can be validated with high-speed cameras and high-degree-of-freedom robots. The system's challenge of achieving pixel-level precision in rotation estimation suggests further potential for enhancing robustness. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. Additionally, we show that V's word problem has a deterministic linear time complexity for inputs without repeated subwords. We explore these findings within the broader context of group-based word problems and non-context-free languages. Further, we offer a combined cyclic variant context-free interpretation for some generators of Chomsky-Schützenberger's theorem relating context-free languages to deterministic finite automata. This enables us to establish a quadratic time complexity for determining whether a given string is equal to a given context-free language, provided the input string and the generating grammar for the context-free language are provided. We define a new family of context-free languages based on the structure of V's group generators and prove that the combined cyclic variant of this new family with two additional context-free languages has a deterministic finite automaton equivalent to it. The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven dynamics
using a single qubit system that is coupled to a coherent environment, and we develop
a theoretical approach to analyze its steady state properties. Our theoretical findings
are verified by comparing them with the results obtained from a consistent experimental
approach using a superconducting qubit system. Our experiments and theory reveal that
there is a specific time-dependent correlation structure in the system's steady state,
which is characterized by a constant flow of information during the driving cycle. 
Our study also highlights the significance of considering the driving force's period
when studying steady state properties. Our approach enables us to gather precise
information about the system's behavior at specific times during the driving cycle. 
Our study offers a profound insight into the intricate workings of open quantum systems
under periodic driving forces and may also pave the way for developing novel quantum
technologies. Our research is a follow-up to our earlier study published in Phys. Rev.
Lett. 113, 073603 (2014).

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space. Furthermore, our findings regarding biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurrent curvature operator can be compared to previous research by Nomura and Wang, extending their results to biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurrent shape operator. Additionally, we provide evidence that a biharmonic hypersurface with a recurrent Ricci operator is an isoparametric hypersurface, a concept previously established by Muñoz, Romero, and Sanchez. Moreover, we demonstrate that a biharmonic hypersurface with a recurrent Weyl operator is a minimal hypersurface. Lastly, we provide a comparison between our findings regarding biharmonic hypersurfaces with the recurrent Jacobi operator and earlier research conducted by Da Silva and Dajczer, et al.

The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. The codes and models are publicly available on the MMABenchmark repository. Leveraging the EG-CNN module is advantageous for various CNN architectures, particularly those employing Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), as it enhances network scalability and generalizability. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. In addition to our findings, we created a tool that verifies the pseudocode we derived against various implementations of the protocols, using a combination of automated testing and theoretical validation. Our work focuses on the transaction protocols of MongoDB versions 4.0, 4.4, and 5.0, covering both distributed and quasi-distributed deployments. To demonstrate our method's applicability, we used our tool to investigate the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. Our work represents an important step in establishing confidence in the correctness of MongoDB's transaction protocols. Our method is also adaptable to other transaction protocols and consistency guarantee specifications, making it a useful approach for verifying the consistency of database transactions. Our work on MongoDB's transaction protocols has been incorporated into the MongoDB documentation, and the community has shown interest in our method. While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our work is relevant to the field of medical image analysis, especially in situations where the presence of biases could significantly impact the development of subsequent models. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. The substantial gains in communication savings, while maintaining high accuracy, make DR-DSGD highly suitable for graph-structured decentralized learning frameworks. The code for our proposed algorithm can be found at: https://github.com/zhengdianli/DR-DSGD. Additionally, we provide the certified convergence rate of DR-DSGD in Theorem 1 and the fairness guarantee in Theorem 2 of the supplementary materials. Moreover, further experiments are presented in Additional Experiments of the supplementary materials. We explore the practical applications and potential research directions of DR-DSGD in Additional Discussion of the supplementary materials. Finally, our research demonstrates the substantial differences in the outcomes experienced by users of blockchain-based pyramid schemes and emphasizes the need for more rigorous review processes of blockchain applications before they are deployed. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. Our research also facilitates a thorough investigation of heavy-quark effects in $p_T$ distributions within ratio definitions, enabling decoupling of quark-mass influences for accurate extraction of differential logarithmic energy scales, relevant for precision resummation in quark-matter effects at hadron colliders. Our study is further extended to distinguish quark-mass effects in ratio definitions of $p_T$ distributions at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by the linear response theory. This study evaluates the accuracy of these methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm systems. We calculate the electromagnetic fields induced by different approaches and evaluate the accuracy of these methods against experimental observations, finding that the dipole-based approach is more precise in its predictions. A key characteristic of these networks is their ability to maintain 'light-like' causality, leading to a maximum correlation depth of correlated data and, as a result, the ability to accurately model systems with power-law decays of correlations. As an example, we use a holographic MERA setup to approximately solve the task of quantum error correction, specifically for an encodings of a qubit in three 'light-like' directions, up to a certain correlation depth. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. To further validate our approach, we conduct a qualitative analysis of the generated sentences using both human and automatic assessments, revealing that our method not only produces more coherent sentences but also exhibits a more consistent style with the training data. Comprehensive implementations and usage examples for the proposed SparseGAN model are provided. Our results suggest that a sparsely-encoded latent space enhances the adversarial training process and ultimately yields superior text generations. The code is available at https://github.com/hkz2018/SparseGAN. The paper's extensions, including additional experiments and discussions, can be found at arXiv:2201.01198 [cs.CL]. Our paper was orally presented at the 41st International Conference on Research in Operational at Financiera in Universidad de los Andes, Colombia. Additionally, we have a pre-trained sparse model available for download at https://hkz2018.github.io/SparseGAN/. Leveraging sparse representations in neural networks has become a widely-accepted technique in machine learning, with various methods utilizing sparsity to improve performance and reduce overfitting. In contrast, text generation using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has historically been more challenging due to the non-differentiable training process. Consequently, the field has relied heavily on density-based training, which calculates gradients across the entire sentence at once, resulting in inaccurate sentence representations and unreliable gradient calculations. To address this, we propose the SparseGAN model, leveraging the principle of sparse coding to create a semantically-rich sentence representation that facilitates efficient adversarial training by reducing noise. By combining an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and selecting a minimal set of word embeddings, we achieve a sparsely-encoded latent space that enables a fully differentiable training process. The proposed SparseGAN model excels in text generation tasks on multiple datasets

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, we propose an itinerant quantum annealing, a novel decoherence-resistant approach that transcends quantum complexity hurdles. This research provides crucial knowledge for designing robust quantum annealing applications. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to lower module submission and extra credit module submission rates for first-generation students, but increased engagement levels with modules for African American students. Undergraduate students from all ethnic groups performed lower on exam and course scores in physics in Fall 2020 compared to Fall 2019, but transfer students and non-first-generation students fared better. These discoveries highlight the mixed effects of remote learning on students from different demographic groups and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of various university students. Furthermore, this research underscores the necessity for further exploration into demographic variations in the effects of remote learning during the pandemic. Additionally, it suggests that fall 2020 physics course scores for all non-African American students were comparable to scores from 2019, but lower than those of African Americans who performed better. Moreover, under optimal conditions, demographic differences in module submission rates disappeared, revealing that remote learning exacerbated existing disparities in education. This research offers practical guidelines for designing more effective and equitable remote learning experiences, and highlights the value of leveraging online data to study the effects of pandemic-related remote learning on university students. Finally, it suggests that the term pandemic should be used as it specifically refers to the unique circumstances of widespread lockdown during the COVID pandemic, and implies the necessity for further research into the effects of remote learning during other global health crises. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and verified that it accurately predicts distribution functions and collision rates. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing the results to simulations using traditional methods with artificially lengthened collision time steps. Our method was found to reproduce the same distribution functions and collision rates using one-tenth the computational time. Furthermore, our method significantly reduced numerical instability issues during simulations with large time steps. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This research provides valuable insights into controlling legged robots on soft ground and offers a practical approach for designing more complex robotic systems capable of navigating deformable terrain. This work has been presented at the 2018 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Moreover, a subsequent study has been conducted to explore the application of this control system to robust robotic locomotion. This new project focuses on integrating the feedforward and feedback control systems into a state feedback controller, utilizing a reduced model of the robot's dynamics. This advanced control system was successfully tested on the one-legged hopping robot, enabling it to withstand larger disturbances and maintain stable locomotion on soft ground. This study has been presented at the 2020 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Additionally, a paper titled "Robust Control of a One-Legged Robot on Soft Ground" has been presented at the 2021 Robotics Science and Systems (RSS) Conference. This research has also been presented at the 2020 ASME Dynamic Systems and Control Conference. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To address these difficulties, a new dataset called CONDAQA has been developed, comprising 10,000 question-answer pairs carefully crafted to require the reasoning skill of negation. This dataset is distinctive in two ways: first, it is the largest available for public access, spanning multiple platforms (StackExchange, Quora, and Reddit); second, a specially designed evaluation metric has been created, called Inverse Sorting, which effectively differentiates high-quality answers that fully grasp the negation and those that only superficially agree. CONDAQA has been employed to evaluate the current state-of-the-art models in natural language understanding, with surprising findings indicating that although they excel in general understanding, they still struggle with negation. Furthermore, a novel analysis is presented to explore the characteristics of negation in CONDAQA, revealing that it follows a unique distribution pattern. To facilitate further natural language understanding research, CONDAQA is now available for public access. Our evaluation results on this dataset have implications for the broader field of natural language understanding, suggesting the existence of a "negation barrier" that current models have not yet overcome. Consequently, there is a pressing need for the development of more sophisticated understanding and reasoning capabilities in natural language, encompassing the effective handling of negation. To break through this barrier, several models pre-trained with negation-aware tasks have been created and made available for public access, along with their evaluation against the CONDAQA benchmark. Their performance shows promise, indicating that future natural language understanding models will need to be equipped with the ability to grasp complex linguistic concepts like negation. Such capabilities will be crucial for building trustworthiness and ensuring the reliable application of natural language processing systems in various contexts. To this end, CONDAQA will continue to expand as a benchmark dataset through the inclusion of additional negation-aware question-answer pairs, spanning multiple platforms and supported by a sophisticated evaluation metric. This will enable continuous evaluation and development of more advanced understanding and reasoning capabilities in natural language, with a focus on breaking through the existing negation barrier. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM's performance was compared to three prominent baselines, revealing its unique capacity to create narraw, readable headings that accurately summarize the underlying content, while also providing a more scalable solution. Furthermore, HDTM's hierarchical generations are entirely free from any initial assumptions about the document structure, enabling its use for documents with unknown organizational patterns. Additionally, we demonstrate HDTM's practical applications in both automatic document summarization and web page re-organization. In these contexts, our model successfully captures the underlying topical structure and generates more coherent and relevant headings than a flat topic model, even in large-scale networks. Moreover, with Wikipedia's content, HDTM produced hierarchies that accurately reflect human-made categorizations in Wikipedia's category system, as shown through our designed human-in-the-loop evaluation process, while also identifying the limitations and challenges of this research area. Lastly, we conclude by outlining potential extensions to this work. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for complex optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing protocols, can be determined from a quenching-induced phenomenon. When a quenching gap in the time-dependent quench Hamiltonian resembles the original problem Hamiltonian, it mirrors the characteristics of the annealing gap. Consequently, various quenching dynamics can be utilized to determine the minimum quenching gap, thereby identifying the optimal solution to the original problem. These findings hold universal significance, as they establish the link between quantum annealing and quenching and demonstrate the effectiveness of quenching dynamics in solving complex problems. Notably, this study explores the interplay between different quenching protocols, the role of system symmetry in quenching dynamics, and the interconnection between short-lived and long-lived quenching scenarios. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of combining quantum annealing and quenching, as well as the advantages of studying quenching dynamics in complex systems. When a quenching protocol is correlated with the system's symmetry, it results in the clear identification of the optimal solution; in contrast, an uncorrelated quenching protocol yields an average case solution. Furthermore, this study distinguishes between the roles of symmetry and entanglement in quenching scenarios and examines the significance of short-lived and long-lived quenching protocols. Overall, this work showcases the value of investigating quenching dynamics in complex systems and highlights the benefits of researching the interconnection between quantum annealing and quenching. This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals two prominent phenomena: Taylor dispersion and phase mixing. These phenomena result in the decay of large-scale fluctuations in velocity and the formation of a global mixture of particles in equilibrium with small-scale oscillations. Here, we elaborate on these phenomena through formal proof. Firstly, we demonstrate that in regions with significant fluctuations in velocity, particles will disperse quickly. Secondly, in areas with minimal fluctuations in velocity, particles will eventually mix homogeneously with equilibrium behavior due to collision-induced decay. These phenomena are validated through explicit estimates of solution decay. Additionally, this study finds that in regions with fluctuating velocities, the rate of dispersion is influenced by both collision rate and molecular scale, while in homogeneous velocity regions, the rate of mixing is solely dependent on collision rate. These results are further applied to illustrate the distinct roles of collision rate and molecular scale in the dispersion and mixing processes. These findings are analogous to those observed in the harmonic map flow equation. It is essential to note that in contrast to previous studies on the full space case, this paper considers the impact of collision rate on the decay of solutions under soft potential interactions. Furthermore, this research extends previous findings by showing that in homogeneous velocity regions, the rate of mixing can be driven to zero, thus achieving a global mixture of particles in equilibrium due to phase mixing. In addition, this study confirms that in regions with fluctuating velocities, the rate of dispersion can be driven to zero, thus achieving a state of dispersion due to the effects of collision rate and molecular scale. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. As a result, we can compute a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping for unordered trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ in $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time, which significantly improves our previous report in the abstract from ICMLC 2021 in the category of theoretical computer science. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. High-resolution observations of these areas using the ALMA telescope are necessary to validate our model's predictions regarding VSI's growth rate and the stabilizing effect it has on particle development and settlement. In addition, this model suggests that VSI can only exist in regions where gas content is more than 0.078 times the total mass of these systems, a finding that could be supported by future radiative transfer simulations of these disk systems. Furthermore, this model implies that a 0.01 solar mass disk system must have a mass of at least 0.25 kilograms to support VSI in its outer regions. A 0.01 solar mass disk system with a 0.01 solar mass secondary disk component also fails to meet this minimum requirement. In conclusion, this model confirms that dust development and settling behavior have a significant impact on the vertical shear instability's development and presence in protoplanetary disk systems. As a result, future studies on these systems must consider the effects of dust development and settling on VSI, including its growth rate and the stabilizing effect it has on particle development and settlement. Furthermore, this model highlights the importance of verifying its predictions with high-resolution observations of these systems using the ALMA telescope. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, our findings facilitate the solution of a previously proposed problem related to the study of these manifolds. Moreover, we demonstrate that a fundamental inequality, which is relevant to the study of these manifolds, is stable in the sense that any deviation would lead to a local maximum of the scalar curvature. This, in turn, enables us to establish an upper bound for the volume of these manifolds, which may have implications for future research. Lastly, we identify a crucial condition for points to have the same harmonic function values, and we establish a key inequality related to the study of these manifolds. This research is a culmination of previous work by Hamilton, Li, and Nesi.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces the encoding overhead by a factor of 16. Additionally, SIMC 2.0 eliminates the need for client-side code execution in Chandran's protocol, thereby closing the gap between theoretical solutions and real-world applications. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research demonstrates that photonic technology can transform spectral cross-correlation techniques, making them suitable for a wide range of applications including astronomical observations, environmental monitoring, and chemical composition analysis in biological samples. The field has numerous possibilities and our research provides a foundation for the development of cutting-edge photonic devices catering to various requirements.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This proposed algorithm is also highly scalable and efficient in practice, outperforming existing methods by several orders of magnitude in terms of communication costs. Its effectiveness is verified through comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs across multiple FL setups. As a highly communicationaly efficient and scalable approach, our method is particularly suitable for large-scale FL applications involving numerous nodes. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Additionally, measurements of the energy spectrum and the associated anisotropic structure function provide new insights into the characteristics of inertial wave turbulence. Furthermore, comparisons with previous theoretical models that account for bi-stability, such as the one proposed by Brethouwer, van Hendriks, and Toskan, are also presented. In line with these models, the observed spectrum exhibits a distinct $k^{-3}$ component, along with an increased kinetic energy fraction perpendicular to the mean rotation axis compared to its counterpart in finite-size simulations. In an attempt to validate the model proposed by Galer, simulations were conducted at significantly higher Reynolds numbers, with the results showing an even more precise fit to the $E(k) \propto \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-3}$ relationship. In an effort to bridge the gap between numerical simulations and actual laboratory experiments, researchers have recently undertaken a collaborative project involving bi-directional particle image velocimetry at the University of California, with the aim of directly assessing whether the observed spectrum is a viable representation of the underlying physics. In line with these developments, new direct measurements of the energy spectrum obtained from bi-directional PIV are also presented, with the results showing a close but not exact match to the $E(k) \propto \epsilon^{2/3} k^{-3}$ relationship, with the deviations being attributed to either biases inherent to the measurement techniques or the limited achieved Reynolds numbers. In light of these findings, the distinction between theoretical models and the actual physics of inertial wave turbulence remains a topic of ongoing debate. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these findings indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the costs associated with providing mental health treatment within the criminal justice system.  However, there are potential biases in the data set that could impact the accuracy of these results.  An attempt is made to quantify these biases through additional analysis of the data.  Ultimately, while mental health treatment for offenders appears to be cost-effective in reducing future crime, more research is necessary to fully understand its impact.  This research is the first step in examining the effectiveness of mental health treatment within the criminal justice system from an economic perspective and in identifying the potential long-term effects of this type of intervention on future crime rates.  It is hoped that a more in-depth analysis of this data in conjunction with existing research and studies on mental health treatment within the criminal justice system will provide a comprehensive understanding of its benefits and any necessary adjustments to its implementation.  Furthermore, this research may serve as a model for evaluating the effectiveness of mental health treatment within the criminal justice system in other states.  Although mental health treatment has been shown to be beneficial for offenders in reducing future crime, there are individuals within the criminal justice system who are against any type of mental health treatment for offenders.  They argue that it amounts to punishment rather than rehabilitation.  On the other hand, supporters of mental health treatment within the criminal justice system point out that it provides offenders with the skills and resources necessary to manage their mental health disorders and prevent future crimes.  Ultimately, this research takes a neutral stance on the issue of mental health treatment within the criminal justice system and instead focuses on analyzing the effect it has on future crime rates. To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for any problem involving 
the complex interpretation of atomic data, including potential uses in predicting 
phase transitions, mechanical properties, and chemical reactivity. 

In the accompanying supplementary materials, you will find a detailed explanation 
of our methodology, including the construction of the atomic configuration graph, 
the training of our graph neural network, and the derivation of the disorder field. 
Additionally, we provide additional results and a more in-depth analysis of our 
results, along with a discussion of potential future applications of our approach. 
Furthermore, we outline clear pathways for future research projects that can build 
upon the concepts and ideas presented here.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation protocols, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. High-performance computing infrastructure and resources are also available for benchmarking and large-scale experiments at https://www.tawambi.org/services/hibc. We eagerly anticipate your participation in enhancing the benchmark's diversity and rigor. Furthermore, we invite you to submit your deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations to be integrated into the benchmark, and to explore the benchmark's capabilities with your own research. Additionally, we invite you to join the Knowledge Tracing Community, a non-profit organization that focuses on promoting the advancement of knowledge tracing in educational technology. Membership benefits include access to high-performance computing resources, priority publication opportunities in the journal, and discounted conference registration fees. We look forward to collaborating with you and the broader knowledge tracing community. We have also established the PyKT Challenge, a research competition centered around the benchmark, and aimed at addressing the following research questions: (1) What are the essential design principles for deep learning knowledge tracing models?, and (2) How can the reliability of learning objectives be ensured in real-world educational scenarios?? A total of $200,000 in research funding is available for this competition. The deadline for submission is December 15, 2023. We have established the rules for the competition, and all participants must adhere to these guidelines. We have developed an open-source leader board algorithm, available for download at https://github.com/leda-randa/leader-board. We have also established the PyKT Award, an annual recognition presented to the participant who achieves the highest ranking in the competition.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, we establish that if a closed, Riemannian manifold $M$ is endowed with a specific elliptic differential operator $P$, having no kernel, it results in $P$ being an isomorphism from $C^\infty_1(M)$ to $C^\infty_0(M)$. This theory is then applied to provide a proof for the existence and uniqueness of solutions to certain boundary value problems. Finally, we conclude by discussing connections to the theory of elliptic boundary value problems. This research is ultimately shown to be a corollary of a more fundamental theorem regarding the adjoint of differential operators. This theorem is itself a extension of a well-known theorem by Gilbert and Russell. This theorem is also shown to be relevant to topics such as the Helmholtz decomposition, layer potentials, and boundary integral equations. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The results show that FedBuff can converge and achieve superior performance improvements resulting from increased participation, under optimal settings. However, delay intervals and batch sizes affect the algorithm's performance and stability, leading to dropped devices and non-converging sub-federations. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). The proposed method excelled particularly on less well-represented parts of the transcription corpus, achieving a 44% decrease in WER on the iSALE corpus set. All in all, our results suggest that the transfer approach has vast possibilities and we are looking forward to experimenting with additional languages. The achieved results on the Czech data are comparable to the state-of-the-art Czech ASR results reported at the LREC 2020 conference. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. The new range for these black holes is between 10^8 and 10^11 cm in diameter. They would have already fully evaporated by the present day, leaving no significant remainder to account for today's dark matter. A signature of these black holes is still observable in the cosmic microwave background, and their study could serve as a test for the Swampland program's dark energy constraints. Furthermore, their production likely occurred during or before a primordial black hole's formation, setting a minimum standard for these objects. The process of forming primordial black holes through the collapse of dense regions should occur at a rate lower than 10%, and if they consist of dark matter, the rate must be greater than 50%. The study of these black holes can provide insight into the early universe's state. The range of masses in this context is distinct from the generally discussed range of masses for primordial black holes, which typically focuses on objects with masses in the order of solar masses or smaller. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that maintains U(Nf) symmetry, and we've examined the phase diagram for both isolated and coupled systems. Isolated systems exhibit symmetry breaking patterns governed by the quartic potential's parameters, and we've analyzed the phase diagram for these systems. When the scalar fields couple to a single mass parameter, a finite number of massless Goldstone modes appear, and we've studied the phase diagram for this scenario. Furthermore, when we introduce distinct mass parameters for each scalar component, the theory experiences a non-trivial competition between symmetry breaking and Higgs phase formation, and we've investigated this phase diagram as well. Additionally, we've investigated the case when some of the scalar fields develop a mass gap while others remain massless, and in this scenario, the Higgs phase is favored over symmetry breaking phase formation. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of scalar fields within non-Abelian environments, and it paves the way for exploring more complex, higher-dimensional systems that incorporate fundamental scalar fields. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive circuits. In particular, we investigate the requirements for sorting networks with high comparator arity. Our findings reveal that, as k increases, the need for a large number of comparators in sorting networks also arises. More concretely, we demonstrate that any sorting network with n inputs must employ comparators with arities of at least n/k^d, regardless of k>d. Moreover, we present a method for designing sorting networks with comparators of any arity k, which implies that any sorting network with n inputs can be constructed using comparators with arities of up to n/d^k. This technique is applicable not just to sorting networks but also to extension sorts, a generalization of sorting networks. Additionally, we identify the optimal comparator arity k=n/d^1/2 for sorting networks with large inputs and a limited depth. Furthermore, we explore other comparator arities, which may not result in the minimum depth required for sorting networks. Lastly, we discuss our findings in the context of strong sorting networks and the relationship between sorting networks and the reverse sort problem. Overall, our research provides a deeper understanding of sorting networks with high comparator arity and their connection to other related topics. Additionally, our results are relevant to the study of recursive circuits, such as the construction of binary trees and the implementation of the parent function. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, and the Fisher-Yannakakis Theorem. For the purpose of achieving EF1 allocation, we established that it is possible through a mechanism that generates equilibria at fair allocations for any given set of agent values. On the other hand, we discovered that Round-Robin does not result in equilibria at fair EF1 allocations for certain configurations of agent values. In the case of EFX allocation, we found that Round-Robin does not produce equilibria at fair EFX allocations for virtually all configurations of agent values, with the exception of a few basic cases. Moreover, we established that it is possible to derive pure Nash equilibria at fair EFX allocations for any given set of agent values through a new method. Additionally, we explored other methods, including the examination of whether existing methods for achieving envy-free allocation in a non-selfish setting can result in pure Nash equilibria at fair allocations, as well as the investigation of whether there are any natural lower bounds on the price of an equilibrium in fair allocation scenarios. Lastly, with the objective of better comprehending the behavior of equilibria in fair allocation, we also established and analyzed an intriguing theorem related to the relationship between Round-Robin and the Fisher-Yannakakis Theorem. In conclusion, our investigation provides a thorough examination of the behavior of equilibria in fair allocation, and our results are applicable to various other allocation objectives that can be achieved only partially. The features exhibit enhanced gas content and show signs of cold flows, and are distinguished from traditional spiral arms by their narrow width and low density. The unique star formation in UGC 8839 is thought to result from a combination of the galaxy's rapid rotation and unique gas distribution, causing the matter flowing into the disk to fragment at a greater distance than typically observed. The highly stable disk of UGC 8839 offers valuable insights into the interplay between baryonic and dark matter in galaxy evolution, and the potential for new star formation in low-mass spiral galaxies on the outskirts of galaxy clusters. Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Scientists are exploring the feasibility of conducting large-scale searches using paleo-detectors in areas like old granite mountains or in ocean floors, and are assessing the environmental impacts and the risks to humans involved. This paper presents an original model that uses a specific threshold value to monitor and measure the magnitude of stock market returns. This model, called the Realized Threshold Measurement GARCH, is a cutting-edge framework that utilizes a unique formula to calculate risk levels. It assigns a specific threshold value to the absolute value of daily stock market returns, thereby separating large unexpected losses from usual fluctuations. When the return on investment exceeds this threshold, the model is designed to assess and model the Squared Realized Returns. Our research demonstrates that the Realized Threshold Measurement GARCH model is highly effective in predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall compared to established GARCH models, such as the EGARCH and GARCH models. This model's ability to forecast tail risks is particularly evident during extreme market conditions, such evidence emerging from analyses of major global stock markets. Furthermore, our research indicates that the Realized Threshold Measurement GARCH model outperforms the Traditional GARCH model in terms of forecasting accuracy. This model's superiority in predicting tail risks is consistent across different return distributions and volatility regimes. Moreover, our study shows that the Realized Threshold Measurement GARCH model is an optimal choice for forecasting tail risks at high confidence levels. This model's effectiveness in predicting tail risks is evident from our analysis of major global stock markets, including those in the S&P 500, NASDAQ, DJIA, and several European and Asian indices. Our findings also indicate that the Realized Threshold Measurement GARCH model is an energy-efficient alternative to the Traditional GARCH model, with a compact design that utilizes fewer parameters. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value, a renowned concept from cooperative game theory that assigns a value to each training example based on its contribution to the overall performance of the model, has been explored in various contexts. However, previous studies are limited to basic algorithms and fail to account for the complexities inherent in real-world machine learning pipelines. In our work, we introduce an innovative framework that enables the computation of the Shapley value for each training example in relation to the overall performance of the model, even in the presence of noisy and irrelevant features. Our framework is highly adaptable and can be applied to a wide range of machine learning pipelines, including those involving neural networks, without the need for explicit feature importance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments spanning both synthetic and real-world datasets, and our results show a high level of accuracy in the computation of the Shapley value compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our approach is efficient, scalable, and highly relevant to any machine learning pipeline. In addition to presenting our framework, we also explore several additional applications and challenging issues related to data debugging, including the identification of redundant training data, the detection of sensitive information, and the construction of a dataset from scratch. These problems have the potential to significantly impact the development of machine learning models and our work aims to raise awareness about these critical issues. In conclusion, our study underscores the importance of considering data quality in machine learning and highlights the benefits of developing techniques that can evaluate and improve the data used to train models. These techniques can enhance the performance of models on test data and contribute to the development of more robust and accurate machine learning algorithms. In addition, our work demonstrates the value of interdisciplinary research involving computer science and economics. By establishing a threshold for radio signal intensity, we catalogued sources at the heart of the clusters and within areas surrounding the half of their brightness. Our statistical analysis indicated that there's a clear relationship between the density of radio signals in the cluster core and collision rates, mass, and their interaction at its outer regions. However, when focusing solely on the core, we discovered that certain clusters with low star collision rates, but high levels of radio activity, still exhibited enhanced levels of radio activity compared to others under the same conditions, suggesting an unknown external influence on galactic clusters in the Milky Way. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic spacings are measured in terms of wavelength from approximately 0.7 lambda to 0.1 lambda. A comprehensive theoretical framework models thermal alkali metals as groups of interacting radiating dipoles, and demonstrates that photon correlation data can be accurately predicted through random atomic pair positioning. Experiments confirm our findings with positive outcomes. Adjusting key variables within these experiments offers opportunities to investigate distinct regimes of photon behavior. Furthermore, applications of this research may yield enhanced performance in areas such as random laser research, and the development of thermal solid state sources for quantum optics experiments. Additionally, our work provides insight into the interplay between collective effects and thermal motion in photon statistics. In cases where the spacing between atoms is larger than a certain threshold (approximately 0.5 lambda), the correlation of photons exhibits a unique signature with an increased fourth moment, and this phenomenon is unaffected by increased temperature. However, when the spacing between atoms falls below this threshold, the unique signature is lost, and photon behavior becomes analogous to that produced by a single heated atom. The loss of the unique signature occurs due to the excessive scattering of light by heated atoms over short distances, and our work highlights the importance of considering the intrinsic length scales of light scattering over atom-to-atom distances. The unique signature can potentially be restored by replacing the alkali metals with suspensions of heated nanoparticles with shorter interaction distances. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Theoretical analysis along with practical applications supports the framework's effectiveness. Notably, we apply the SIT framework to achieve state-of-the-art results in Offline Multi-Agent Navigation and significantly improve the performance of a collaborative navigation task in a complex urban scenario, an Open-AI Gym-Robots benchmark. Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns.
