Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content, as well as the role of contextual factors such as score range, bias, and distribution. Our findings show that although automated essay scoring systems claim to base their decisions on objective content, they are actually heavily influenced by subjective labels. We also discovered that these systems often overreact to minor changes in input, resulting in significantly altered output. In response to these issues, we developed a mathematical model that highlights the impracticality of current score scales and proposed several potential solutions, including score normalization and the use of generative models. These solutions aim to enhance the robustness and reliability of automated essay scoring systems. This research provides a starting point for exploring the intricate workings of complex machine learning models and highlights the importance of open-source scoring models that facilitate both understanding and manipulation. This paper also raises critical questions about the use of similar models in other high-stakes applications. Finally, our results demonstrate that machine learning models with similar characteristics, such as fluid dynamics models, can be manipulated in a comparable manner. This has significant implications for the growing practice of leveraging machine learning models that prioritize performance over interpretability. This research has far-reaching implications for the use of machine learning models in settings where decisions are made based on ratings or scores. This is because a core aspect of modeling human behavior involves capturing the inherent subjectivity and variability of human responses. This research has been conducted with the guidance of leading machine learning researchers, automated scoring system developers, and experts in human behavior modeling. This work will be further expanded to incorporate additional machine learning model explanations and human behavior modeling techniques. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded promising results. However, these models usually have limited generalizability and tend to struggle with overfitting. In an effort to address these challenges and achieve high accuracy in nucleus segmentation, the authors present a new framework called W-Net, which incorporates two stages of convolutional neural networks. In the first stage, the network aims to segment the entire cell based on the boundary of the nucleus, while in the second stage, it refines the segmentation by utilizing the results from the first stage along with additional information from a fully convolutional network. The authors evaluated their model on a publicly available dataset for colon nucleus segmentation and compared its performance to state-of-the-art point-annotated baselines, demonstrating its superiority in terms of accuracy. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the activation of NLRP3 inflammasomes, which can be stimulated by SARS-CoV-2 infection.  Once activated, the NLRP3 inflammasome leads to the self-catalyzed processing of pro-caspase-1 into active caspase-1, resulting in the cleavage of gasdermin family proteins and the release of inflammatory mediators.  Building on existing research, we developed a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the dynamics of pyroptosis and inflammation following SARS-CoV-2 infection.  Our model incorporates key biological processes and cell state transitions, including the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, the processing of pro-caspase-1, and the resulting cell death and inflammation.  We then used our model to investigate the effects of different interventions aimed at reducing inflammation, including targeting the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and gasdermin.  Our analysis reveals how these interventions impact the distribution of cell states, inflammation levels, and overall mortality rates.  Furthermore, our model demonstrates that the optimal intervention strategy depends on multiple factors, including the duration of infection and individual variability between cells.  We believe that our model will contribute to the ongoing search for effective treatments against COVID-19 and other inflammatory diseases.  It has been made publicly available to facilitate collaboration and further research.  In addition, we have included numerical solutions to avoid numerical singularity at the start of infection.  In its current form, our model represents a single-compartment model, focusing on a collection of cells rather than an entire organ or the broader population.  As such, it is known as a mean-field model.  As research on single-cell models continues to advance, we are open to exploring multi-compartment models that account for different cell types within an organ or tissue. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. This project is initially applied to the development of a static checker for Michelson contracts with a cyclic digital signature feature and is currently being utilized in production on the Tezos blockchain as part of the Bitesize contract competition. Further information on HELMHOLTZ can be found at https://helmholtz.ligom.org/. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Finally, the intuition gained from this analysis is applied to the examination of GCNNs in order to derive a formula that predicts any GCNN layer's output, thereby bypassing the need for explicit parameter visualization. This prediction formula holds relevance to the network's training, offering a perspective that could guide future research in this domain. This exploration of GCNNs provides a clear and accessible understanding of these complex networks, building on the matched filtering concept initially introduced in our prior study of standard CNNs. This research on GCNNs complements that prior work, extending the matched filtering framework to address the unique characteristics and challenges posed by graph-ordered data. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This idea is illustrated through a simple example drawn from reachability analysis in algorithms. Additionally, we explore how to maintain the safety property by re-expressing the property as a set of inequalities and incorporating the cut steps into the pseudocodes as additional predicates with the same computational power as the original algorithms. This is demonstrated using the example of solving systems of linear equations. Furthermore, we investigate the expressiveness of our approach by showing an example of an infeasible cut-sensitive proof, and we discuss how our approach can be applied to other domains with computational rules. This research is an initial exploration of the concept of logical pseudocodes, and we anticipate that this approach can be useful for other applications such as the discovery of new algorithms, teeming as it does with computational rules and proofs. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. We also empirically demonstrate the robustness of our approach to various adversary tactics and strategy update frequencies. Our method and associated data are publicly available online. This hierarchical framework may also be applicable to adapting existing pursuit-evasion algorithms for use in other hierarchical reinforcement learning applications. Furthermore, we find that our approach overcomes the significant challenge of balancing exploration-exploitation across a large grid world by localized focus on individual states. We also observe that our method can be connected to value-decomposition techniques used in multi-agent reinforcement learning. As a result of its efficient computations, our approach may be a suitable foundation for real-world large-scale game applications. Finally, we discuss how our method can be used in collaborative settings and provide an initial analysis of its performance. Through further development and optimization of our approach, we achieve an even more significant computational speedup, but this improvement is shown to be susceptible to grid size variability. Ultimately, our method holds promise for real-world large-scale game applications requiring efficient computations. In conclusion, our hierarchical framework offers an superior solution for large-scale stochastic pursuit-evasion games by balancing computational efficiency and actual performance. Last, we highlight potential future research directions for hierarchical reinforcement learning in complex grid worlds. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at preserving image details while reducing noise. A popular deep learning approach called the unsupervised cycleGAN framework has emerged as a leading method for noise reduction in low-dose CT images. However, the use of two separate neural networks in this framework greatly increases neural network parameters, training time, and computational cost. This paper introduces a new modification to the cycleGAN framework called the AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN, which simplifies the neural network architecture while maintaining equivalent performance. The proposed framework was evaluated using a dataset of standard-dose CT images and successfully applied to low-dose CT image denoising. Comparison with the original cycleGAN framework revealed a 38% reduction in neural network parameters, with no noticeable degradation in image quality. Further verification was conducted with a separate dataset of low-dose CT images, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness in preserving image structure and quality. The results indicate that the proposed framework achieves comparable visual quality to the original cycleGAN framework, with a significantly reduced number of neural network parameters. Introduction of adaptive instance normalization allowed for seamless switching between the forward and reverse mappings of the neural network, enabling equal performance with half the number of neural network parameters. Introduction of this layer resolved the notable artifacts present in previously published cycleGAN-based images, replacing them with natural texture and structure. As a result, the proposed framework offers a more efficient and practical solution for enhancing low-dose CT images while preserving natural texture and structure. Further analysis of the results with an expert radiologist confirmed that the proposed framework's images are suitable for accurate diagnosis. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this limitation, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all available labeled data for supervision. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs while pushing together semantically related dialogs apart. To optimize the STS, a novel multi-view contrastive loss function is designed to leverage both labeled and unlabeled dialogs. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects that permit rotational states with distinct multiplicities to coexist and interact. Furthermore, we observe rotational states in $^{42}$Mg to conform with a linear rotational pattern, whereas in $^{44}$Mg, a non-linear rotational pattern prevails. Both findings are linked to differences in total angular momentum and the resultant multi-state coupling that arises from an interplay between pair correlations and the rotation of the nucleus. Consequently, identifying and separating different processes becomes a significant challenge. Consequently, the Effective Vector Boson Approximation (EVA) has been widely adopted to enhance the likelihood of detecting certain processes, specifically those involving $W$ and $Z$ bosons in high-energy muon collisions. Initially developed for large center-of-mass energies, the EVA now needs to be re-evaluate for its applicability in next-generation muon colliders operating at 3-5 TeV. Theoretical predictions, specifically for the irreducible diboson process, indicate that using the EVA at these energies yields cross section estimations 1.5 times the actual value for certain processes. Furthermore, the EVA splits the mass spectrum of irreducible triboson production, contributing significantly to the model's accuracy. To utilize the EVA effectively, studying the characteristics of the EVA model is essential, specifically its dependence on the collider's beam properties. It is crucial to choose the optimal value for the EVA's form factor $\chi$ to obtain the most accurate results. The solutions for $\chi$ are provided for both two-body and three-body processes to guarantee the EVA's validity in future experiments and to establish a more precise understanding of its properties. The study of triboson production in muon collisions using the EVA also reveals new supralinear mass effects, leading to a significant increase in mass differences by as much as 1.5 GeV in certain cases, which could pose a challenge in accurately determining the mass of heavy particles in future experiments. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach through both
simulated and real-world experiments on multiple reinforcement learning scenarios
and datasets, observing the detrimental effects of shared models and the benefits
of our proposed sub-network architecture. Our results indicate that this
approach achieves the best balance between efficiency and effectiveness, matching or
exceeding the performance of model-free multi-task reinforcement learning methods.
We also explore the generalization capabilities of these sub-networks through a
robustness analysis, demonstrating that their performance is stable across various
perturbations. Our study's findings are significant, as they highlight the
differences between model-free and model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
settings and the importance of considering catastrophe interference in model-based
learning. Our proposed sub-network architecture provides a solution to this
issue, and it has the potential to be applied to other contexts where shared
representations are beneficial. Additionally, we believe that our results will
be of use to the broader reinforcement learning community, as they raise important
questions about the benefits of shared representations in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Our study's findings also inspire the creation
of the Multi-Task Low-Fidelity Benchmark, a comprehensive evaluation of the
performance of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning methods using low-
fidelity evaluation criteria. This benchmark allows for the assessment of
robustness and generalization in reinforcement learning scenarios. We make all of

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. At the heart lies the potent combination of the Axiom of Choice and the Compactness Theorem, enabling the construction of key properties through the application of the Diagonal Lemma. Our work demonstrates that in the context of first-order logic, all aforementioned results can be derived from just two fundamental lemmas: the Diagonal Lemma and the utilization of the Axiom of Choice (equivalent to the Compactness Theorem). We further explore the extensions of these results to other formal systems and the role of the Axiom of Choice in them. Our work is entirely self-contained, with all necessary derivations included for the involved theorems and lemmas. We also examine the historical context of these theorems and the development of modern constructive logic. Finally, we explore an intriguing connection between the Godel's first incompleteness theorem and the Halting problem. Our work is a comprehensive exploration of the common foundation that underlies some of the most influential theorems in the history of logic and computability theory. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. These investigations provide insight into the possibilities and limitations of using AI for eye-in-hand calibration, suggesting future research directions in this field. Our findings are particularly relevant to the development of adaptive sampling strategies, which could optimize the calibration process by incorporating previous measurements. 

This research was conducted at the University of Oxford and the University of Edinburgh respectively.

This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. We also showed that our approach matches the theoretical properties of the underlying GAN framework. We shared specific implementation details and the statistical efficiency of our method, which enables the training of complex models with modest computational resources. Ultimately, we highlighted potential applications and future research directions for our proposed technique. We are making our code publicly available to facilitate further exploration and improvement of this approach. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude the discussion by considering implications of these conditions for the structure of boundary equilibrium points in fractional-order systems. Finally, we provide a brief exploration of methods for identifying linear invariant subspaces in fractional-order systems. We anticipate this discussion will contribute to a deeper understanding of the principles and properties of invariant sets in dynamical systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's minimal effect on pulsar signal distortion suggests there are regions of the interstellar medium that, despite containing scattering screens, do not significantly impact the passage of low-frequency radio waves. The detection of this screen also provides insight into the balance of empty space and dense matter in the Local Bubble, indicating that areas of the interstellar medium with reduced density may be more abundant than previously estimated. Furthermore, the absence of screens within a specific angular radius in the scintillation patterns of PSR B1133+16, unlike those of the pulsar PSR B0835-04, implies that the former pulsar is located outside the molecular ring surrounding the Sun, Sago (2020) described as the "Local Pulsar Ring". The screen's location and surrounding environment offer a glimpse into the structure of the local interstellar medium, providing a new perspective for the study of the balance of empty space and dense matter in the Local Bubble through the observation of pulsar scintillations. This research also highlights the value of long-term monitoring of pulsar scintillations, emphasizing the importance of persistent observations in science applications. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Notably, QPNet outperforms baseline WN models in terms of naturalness and exhibits superiority when compared to alternative PDCNN models. Additionally, the model's efficiency and generalizability are discussed. Overall, the proposed quasi-periodic WaveNet presents an appealing solution for the challenging generation of raw waveforms with controllable pitch. Experimental code and demo audio are available at https://github.com/MengQian2015/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. This paper includes an informal discussion of the background and related work, with a formal document available as a supplementary file. Additionally, a voice conversion application based on the proposed cascaded structure is briefly explored. Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on Kepler-452e and two others - HR 5126e and Wolf 1061 c - this work uses a comprehensive atmospheric model to investigate their potential photochemical changes. Initially, the model assessed atmospheres composed of CO2, N2, and CH4, considering stellar radiation from both host stars. Kepler-452e, orbiting a bright G-type star, faces extreme ultraviolet degradation and a significant oxygen loss problem. In contrast, HR 5126e and Wolf 1061 c, around smaller and cooler M-type stars, experience little oxygen depletion. However, all three planets undergo some level of oxygen consumption, and their atmospheric h2o abundances are adversely affected by the same water dissociation process that causes oxygen depletion. As a result, the atmospheric compositions of these planets may appear biologically inactive. Additionally, the model investigated the effects of these photochemical changes on their spectral characteristics and identified potential targets for future biosignature research. Notably, the abundance of CO will be an important indicator, along with other organic molecules, in atmospheres of these exoplanets. Furthermore, the model was used to simulate these planets under different stellar types, such as K and F-type stars, to better understand the impacts of varying host stars on their atmospheres. Lastly, the model was used to assess the capabilities of current and future instruments, such as HiCITE and HiCIAO, to detect the changes it has predicted for these planets. The model also identified water absorption features in spectra obtained from recent observations of these planets, confirming its accuracy. The model will be made available to the scientific community to facilitate the exploration of these planets through spectroscopic analysis. The study of these planets provides valuable insights into the applications and limitations of atmospheric modeling, while the model's predictions and its confirmation of water features in these planets offer a wealth of information for future instrument development and exoplanetary research. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with graphs that are naturally hyperbolic in nature. To overcome this limitation, our proposed Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) utilizes the Lorentzian geometry to provide a more accurate representation of graph data, thereby leveraging the benefits of non-Euclidean geometry to enhance the performance of GCNs. By integrating a Lorentzian memory bank into LGCN, we have developed a novel approach to learning geometric representations on graphs, which is particularly effective in comparative classification tasks. Our method's superiority over traditional GCNs is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations conducted on randomly sampled MNIST, as well as comprehensive benchmark tests on corrupted graphs and the Northwestern University Graph Dataset, showcasing substantial gains in multiple metrics. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggests that these water poor isotopic signatures and low contents resulted from the hydration of pyroxene minerals through interaction with hydrated silicate melt, rather than direct accretion of water rich hydrous minerals. This hydration occurred when hydrated melt from accreted silicate rocks interacted with pyroxene minerals at high temperatures during impact melting events on the parent bodies, leading to the formation of water poor hydrous pyroxene. This discovery provides new evidence for the possibility of partial melting and dehydration of planetesimals that accreted during the early stages of solar system formation, supporting a dry rather than a fully wet accretion model of the inner solar system. This finding is consistent with previous melting and metal-silicate differentiation experiments on chondritic samples, and it implies that the inner solar system experienced high degrees of thermal processing, resulting in the dehydration of volatile elements, particularly water. In contrast, outer solar system objects, like Ceres and the outer asteroid belt, are thought to have experienced lower levels of thermal processing and thus retained their water. This distinction in thermal history has left a lasting legacy on the planetary formation process, affecting the final composition and structure of planetary systems. It suggests that multiple small, rapidly accreting objects can form in the early solar nebula, and these objects could have played a significant role in breaking up large planetesimals during the late stages of planetary accretion, also known as planetary fragmentation, also making it possible for large grains to be efficiently removed from accretion disks, thus preventing the over accumulation of volatiles on forming planets.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. We propose an innovative single-stage framework, leveraging neural network technology to directly translate spoken language. Our model builds upon Neural Machine Translation and Multimodal Architecture, incorporating multiple features of spoken language. By utilizing zero-shot translation, our framework enables efficient deployment across multiple languages without language-specific model training. Our experiments demonstrate that this single-stage approach surpasses two-stage methods in multiple language pairs, particularly in languages with limited data. Additionally, our model shows exceptional performance in zero-shot settings, achieving nearly equivalent results to training language-specific models. We also observe a notable improvement in low-resource language pairs when comparing single-stage and two-stage approaches. Our model's efficiency and effectiveness in zero-shot speech translation make it a promising solution for translating low-resource languages and languages with limited spoken data. Our findings also suggest the presence of a spoken-language specific challenge, distinct from the spoken-form of written-language, and model's difficulty in capturing this challenge when using the latter. Our models and data are available at https://speechtranslation.github.io/. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. In our experiments and benchmarks, our method demonstrates superior performance and stability compared to traditional methods. In particular, it outperforms NFFT3 by up to 5 times and FFTW by up to 3 times in complex grid computations. In terms of accuracy, our method uses computational units identical to those used in NFFT3, FFTW, and Helsing-Ojala's method. In our implementations, we utilize the Dask library to further enhance our method's performance over grids by up to 10 times when done correctly.
